  Large language model agents can self-improve over time by utilizing procedural memory derived from prior task trajectories, yet the distinct utilities of memories derived from local successes and failures remain underexplored. This work studies this question in a realistic setting with heterogeneous streams of multi-domain tool-use tasks and various environment constraints common in real-world scenarios. We develop \emph{Dual-Polarity Memory with Periodic Maintenance} (DualPM), a simple, retrieval-free memory workflow characterized by (1) customizable reflection and procedural memory generation from both local successes and failures within each trajectory, and (2) periodic memory consolidation over long task streams under a given memory capacity, preventing memory explosion. Online prequential evaluation with fine-grained metrics reveals that failure memory more strongly broadens coverage, success memory better streamlines execution, while combining both polarities effectively integrates both benefits. Further studies demonstrate that DualPM enables cross-domain memory generalization and continual memory adaptation, while external evaluation on EvoMemBench reveals the portability and effectiveness of DualPM as a general long-term procedural memory method.
  </details>

- **[LogToPersona: New Benchmark and Efficient Persona Prediction through Semantic Log Filtering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33510)**  `arXiv:2611.33510`  
  _Ahmed Alajrami, Ondrej Bohdal, Seokwoo Song, Taegeon Um, Peyman Hosseini, Savas Ozkan, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Detailed knowledge of a user's persona is valuable for personalizing generative AI models and agents, yet such details are difficult to obtain and change over time. We address the task of inferring persona attributes from a single day of mobile activity logs. No suitable publicly available benchmark exists for this task, so we introduce a synthetic benchmark of 1,600 persona-log pairs. We target on-device inference so that raw logs never leave the phone, which makes memory rather than speed the limiting constraint: a day of activity yields roughly 30K tokens, whose key-value cache alone exceeds the INT4 weights of a 4B-parameter model. We therefore propose a log filtering method that retains only behaviorally distinct entries. Filtering reduces the memory footprint by up to 39% across nine models from four families and more than halves prefill time, while maintaining or improving prediction quality. For Qwen3-4B it removes 2.5GB, bringing the model from well beyond a realistic per-process budget to a manageable one. Within our benchmark, these results indicate that preserving diverse behavioral events matters more for persona prediction than retaining every semantically similar log entry.
  </details>

- **[Evaluating Large Language Models on conversational African American English: Feature classification and next-turn generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33499)**  `arXiv:2611.33499`  
  _Romeo De Timmerman, Thomas Demeester, Els Lefever_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large Language Models (LLMs) are known to misinterpret and misrepresent regional and social varieties of English other than Mainstream American English (MAE), such as African American English (AAE), yet most evaluations of these biases have relied on synthetic, stylized or decontextualized data. This paper instead evaluates LLMs on authentic, conversational AAE to more closely reflect how such models may encounter AAE when deployed as chatbots. Concretely, we perform two complementary evaluation tasks on 100 six-turn segments randomly sampled from the Corpus of Regional African American Language (CORAAL; Kendall and Farrington, 2024), comparing three closed-weight LLM configurations: Gemini 2.5 Flash with and without reasoning, and GPT-4.1 mini. The first task compares the models against gold-standard manual annotations for five AAE morphosyntactic features, while the second assesses their ability to generate contextually appropriate next turns, evaluating outputs for AAE feature frequency, diversity (Self-BLEU), and pragmatic quality. Reasoning-enabled Gemini is the strongest feature detector by a clear margin (macro F1 of 0.91), outperforming both other LLMs as well as a finetuned BERT-based baseline (Masis et al., 2022). In generation, however, all LLMs underproduce AAE relative to the human speakers and produce relatively uniform continuations, with reasoning-enabled Gemini producing the least AAE and the least diverse output. We conclude that a model's ability to detect AAE does not straightforwardly translate into its spontaneous use of AAE in generation, and argue that addressing this gap requires changes upstream, in how pretraining and alignment data represent dialectal variation.
  </details>

- **[Learning from Recurrence: Internalizing Depth-Induced Preferences in Looped Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33468)**  `arXiv:2611.33468`  
  _Hui Chen, Joshua Elsdon, Can Goksen_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  A looped language model repeatedly applies the same block to its hidden state before predicting each token. The number of passes is its recurrent depth. Increasing this depth gives the model more computation per token with the same parameters. Can the shared block learn from the predictions it makes at greater depth? Following prior work, we retrofit pretrained OLMo-2-1B with a shared recurrent block and continue mid-training over varying recurrent depths. In the four-pass model, additional passes mainly redistribute probability among tokens that already rank highly after one pass. We use the continuations generated at greater depth to train only the shared block through a single pass, without reference answers or correctness filtering. We call this transfer preference write-back. Write-back further improves one-pass and multi-pass accuracy on most tasks. At their target depths, the updated models outperform a non-recurrent control matched for mid-training data and token budget on all six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, with a mean relative gain in accuracy of up to 46.2% across tasks. At four-pass inference, one-pass training outperforms full-depth training on the same targets in the model with input injection. This advantage disappears in the matched model without injection. On GSM8K, using the updated block only on passes two through four recovers nearly the entire four-pass gain, showing that an update learned in one pass can improve later applications of the same block.
  </details>

- **[AI-human hybrid conversations: Can AI Agents Improve Discourse Quality?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33459)**  `arXiv:2611.33459`  
  _Ishita Chakraborty, Xingjian You, Shrabastee Banerjee_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Conversations are central to how people exchange information, share experiences, and develop collective understanding. Yet, across conversational settings, discussions often suffer from uneven participation, unanswered contributions, and a narrow range of perspectives. As generative AI agents increasingly participate alongside humans, hybrid human-AI conversations present a new opportunity to address these challenges. We investigate whether AI agents can serve as catalysts for human interaction, improving conversational engagement and broadening collective discourse. We develop a framework for introducing generic and persona-conditioned AI agents into evolving discussions and evaluate it through two complementary studies. First, using agent-based simulations grounded in Reddit discussions across four domains, we find that AI-generated conversations are more positive and less toxic than human conversations, but substantially less semantically diverse. Persona conditioning produces more human-like contributions and narrows this diversity gap, while increasing the representation of underrepresented personas can shift which perspectives emerge without necessarily increasing overall diversity. Second, we conduct a pre-registered experiment with 221 participants across nine discussion threads, comparing human-only conversations with those involving generic or persona-conditioned AI agents. We find that AI participation increases responsiveness, reduces unanswered contributions, and broadens the range of ideas expressed by human participants, even though the AI agents themselves do not fully reproduce human conversational diversity. These findings suggest that the value of hybrid human-AI conversations lies not simply in the content AI agents generate, but also in their potential to stimulate more responsive and diverse interactions among humans.
  </details>

- **[Open-Source FUTO Keyboard Layouts and Predictive Text for a Few Endangered Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33432)**  `arXiv:2611.33432`  
  _Mika Hämäläinen, Jack Rueter, Khalid Alnajjar_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We present open-source FUTO Keyboard layouts and predictive text dictionaries for five endangered Uralic languages: Erzya, Moksha, Komi-Zyrian, Livonian, and Skolt Sami. Existing Divvun Android keyboard layouts are converted automatically into the YAML format used by FUTO Keyboard. For predictive text, we construct weighted AOSP dictionaries using translated Finnish lemma frequencies together with morphological frequencies extracted from small target-language corpora using finite-state transducers. This combination provides a practical way to rank inflected word forms when large monolingual corpora are unavailable. The resulting resources offer reusable mobile keyboard support for endangered Uralic languages.
  </details>

- **[When the Knowledge Runs Out: A Part-Level Pilot Evaluation of How Language Models Handle Partially Covered Questions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33428)**  `arXiv:2611.33428`  
  _Vahid Mohammadi_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Assistants that answer from supplied reference material often receive material that covers some parts of a user's question and not others. Existing evaluations of insufficient context mostly score one answer per question, and often treat partially sufficient context as simply insufficient. We describe a small, open evaluation that scores each part of a three-part question separately, with a verdict for parts that are answered correctly from the material but carry an added unsupported claim. On 30 cases (five scenarios, six coverage patterns, five samples each) we test claude-haiku-4-5 and llama3.1:8b. Without an explicit instruction to stay within the material, both models fill most gaps from their own knowledge (unsupported-claim rates of 0.71 and 0.90). One added sentence instructing them to answer only from the material brings these rates to 0.00 and 0.06, consistent with prior work. What remains is less visible: answers that strengthen the material, for example turning "many job sites prohibit bots" into a flat "no". We also report on the judge. Three rounds of blind hand labelling show that this added-claim verdict is the hardest to apply, for the judge and the author alike; RAGAS faithfulness is unsuitable for this task because it penalises correct withholding; and a difference between the two models that is clear under one judge disappears when the judge model is replaced. The dataset, code, hand labels and per-run figures are public.
  </details>

- **[Lost in Translation, Not in Confidence: Benchmarking and Calibrating Multilingual Decision Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33307)**  `arXiv:2611.33307`  
  _Mingzhe Du, Thong Thanh Nguyen, Nguyen Tran Cong Duy, See-Kiong Ng, Luu Anh Tuan_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Decision models are language models fine-tuned to return a probability for each option of a typed query, which routers and guardrails threshold directly. They are built on multilingual bases but ranked almost entirely in English. We evaluate 25 top-ranked open-weight decision models on 17 tasks in 14 languages, comparing each language with English on parallel items. Every model loses accuracy in every language, from about 2 points in high-resource languages to 8 in Tamil, while confidence falls only half as much: a threshold set for 95\% accuracy in English yields 90% in Tamil. The size of the loss is set by the language and the base model rather than by leaderboard rank. In 81 controlled fine-tuning runs, task skill learned in English transfers to other languages and a few thousand target-language items narrow large losses, but neither more data nor full-parameter tuning closes them. Finally, the same test items are answered more accurately in all 23 benchmark--language pairs we compare when an LLM rather than a person translated them, so LLM-translated test sets understate the gap.
  </details>

- **[FrIdéo: French News Outlet Ideology Scoring via Multi-Source Evidence Fusion and Distancing-Aware Lexical Scoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33266)**  `arXiv:2611.33266`  
  _Amr Sobhy_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Outlet ideology is a standard explanatory variable in media framing, media effects, and political communication research, but continuous, ecosystem-wide coverage lets it enter as graded exposure rather than a coarse bin. For France, existing references are either broad but non-analytic or analytic but sparse and source-specific, and none we are aware of offers ecosystem-wide coverage on a unified continuous scale. We contribute FrIdéo: to our knowledge the first ecosystem-wide continuous ideology scores for the French press, a transparent composite score for 30 French news outlets, fusing nine independent families of evidence with empirical-Bayes-style shrinkage toward a structural prior. For the text-based family we introduce symmetric plain/qualified scoring, which separates the plain use of ideologically loaded vocabulary from its qualified (distanced) use on both sides, a distinction bag-of-words methods miss. The resulting scale runs from L'Humanité on the far left to Valeurs actuelles on the far right; the far-right pole is near-indistinguishable and CNews ties Le Figaro. Because the text family reads current articles, it also captures editorial change that static sources miss, such as the Journal du Dimanche's sharp rightward shift after its 2023 ownership change. The ordering is robust to perturbation and to dropping any single family, and agrees with held-out Media Bias Fact Check labels. We release the scores, confidence intervals, and replication code.
  </details>

- **[Focus On Facts: Stylistically Invariant and Factually Sensitive Text Embeddings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33250)**  `arXiv:2611.33250`  
  _Maximus Adeola_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Text embedding models can conflate surface-form similarity with factual identity. Given an altered near-copy with one corrupted fact and a differently worded fact-preserving rewrite, the base model prefers the altered near-copy. We test whether hard-negative contrastive supervision can reduce this surface-similarity shortcut. We construct FOF-Bench, an 83,263-triplet benchmark spanning five domains. Each anchor is paired with an LLM-generated, fact-preserving stylistic rewrite and a matched fact-altered near-copy. We fine-tune FOF-80M (Focus On Facts), an 80M-parameter embedding model, with a triplet contrastive objective that ranks the rewrite above the factual alteration. On 8,327 held-out test triplets, the base model chooses the factually altered text in 99.58% of cases (0.42% factual preference rate; mean separation -0.1650). After fine-tuning, mean positive--negative separation is +0.0329, 98.5% of individual margins move in the intended direction, and the preference rate reaches 29.37%. On DiSC, an external style-transfer corpus, mean cross-style similarity increases from 0.7905 to 0.9559. The model also penalizes omission and transfers poorly to directional tasks such as NLI and summarization. We characterize FOF-80M as a soft factual fingerprint for studying factual retention under stylistic variation, not as a general-purpose factuality metric.
  </details>

- **[Extraneous Cognitive Load in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33197)**  `arXiv:2611.33197`  
  _Arushi Gupta, Sheng Liu, James Zou_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) shows that human problem-solving is affected by both intrinsic load, arising from task difficulty, and extraneous load, arising from how task information is presented. Large language models (LLMs) show analogous effects: presentation alone can affect model performance, but these effects have not yet been systematically isolated from task difficulty. To address this gap, we introduce CogLoadBench, a controlled benchmark that varies five CLT-inspired presentation factors across three reasoning task families. Across models, we find that higher extraneous load conditions often reduce accuracy by either adding competition or complicating the reasoning path. To support diagnosis and mitigation of load-related effects, we propose the Extraneous Load Score (ELS), a prompt-time metric computed from activations that estimates a model's extraneous load, and show that it generalizes across reasoning task types and load levels. We further show that shifting model representations toward lower-load directions at inference time can improve average model performance without changing prompt content.
  </details>

- **[Feature-Based Explainability of Transformer Scoring Models: A Fidelity-First Framework for Automated Writing Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33175)**  `arXiv:2611.33175`  
  _Michael Hemenway, Edward W. Wolfe_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Transformer-based automated writing scoring models can achieve strong agreement with human scores while providing limited transparency into the response characteristics associated with their predictions. This study evaluated a feature-based post-hoc explanation approach in which explanatory fidelity was established before feature importance was interpreted. English Language Arts responses from three writing prompts in Grades 6 and 8 were analyzed, with about 12,700 responses per prompt and separate DeBERTa-v3-base research models for Expression and Conventions. Each response was represented by 61 interpretable linguistic and writing-quality features. Four approaches - theory-driven composites, hierarchical feature groupings, exploratory factor analysis, and Random Forest surrogates - were compared in their ability to reproduce DeBERTa predictions. Random Forest surrogates produced the largest observed R2 values across all six prompt-by-trait conditions, with held-out R2 values from .81 to .95. SHAP analyses showed substantial overlap in high-importance features across traits, with 75% to 90% of the top 20 features shared. Trait differentiation occurred mainly through relative feature weighting: Expression showed greater importance for lexical and conceptual indicators, whereas Conventions showed greater importance for sentence-level and syntactic-control indicators. Under researcher-defined mappings, rubric correspondence was 90%-95% for Expression and 12%-18% for Conventions. These percentages are descriptive and conditional on the mappings and available linguistic features. The findings support a fidelity-first framework for examining apparent scoring priorities while distinguishing post-hoc evidence about model behavior from direct explanation of transformer internals.
  </details>

- **[MGMem: An Efficient, Deterministic, and Provenance-Preserving Framework for Long-Horizon Agent Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33174)**  `arXiv:2611.33174`  
  _Junhong Huang, Xin Tong, Jun Xia_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Long-horizon Large Language Model (LLM) agents need persistent memory that surfaces the right past interaction at the right time across thousands of turns. Many systems index by invoking generative LLMs to rewrite history into summaries, facts, or knowledge graphs--a step that is (a) costly (thousands of generative calls per build), (b) non-deterministic (undermining reproducibility and giving inconsistent answers across runs), and (c) provenance-erasing (the reader sees synthesized text, not the original turn). We propose MGMem, a framework with no generative indexing calls that replaces this step with a deterministic discriminative-parser pipeline: recurring mentions across sessions are organized into an incidence graph, question mentions are resolved by a subject-conditioned three-stage resolver, and raw dialogue episodes are returned to the reader. On English multi-session dialogue QA, MGMem outperforms matched-protocol baselines on LoCoMo without generative indexing calls; on the full LongMemEval-S, it remains competitive overall and leads or ties on single-session types among local retrieval comparisons. Code:this https URL
  </details>

- **[Modeling Bilingual Learning Through LLM Training: A Critical-Period Exploration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32997)**  `arXiv:2611.32997`  
  _Uriel Benymon, Tristan Whipps, Armita Ghobadi_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Critical-period accounts of second-language (L2) acquisition suggest that the ability to learn a new language may depend on how easily previously acquired first-language (L1) knowledge can be modified. This exploratory computational study extends a neural language-model approach to critical-period effects by examining internal representations rather than behavior. A small two-layer GPT-2 model was trained on English and then on German (a relatively related L2) or Finnish (a relatively distant L2) through either Sequential training or Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC), which limits change in parameters important for English. Mean-pooled hidden states for 20 held-out probe sentences per language were compared with those of the English-only model using cosine similarity at the embedding layer and two transformer layers after one and two L2 epochs. English similarity remained high in the transformer layers but became negative in the embedding layer. L2 similarity increased in the transformer layers, and German and Finnish differed more in the second transformer layer than in the first. EWC reduced Fisher-weighted parameter drift by about 6% but changed transformer-layer similarity by less than .001. With one training run per condition, these findings are preliminary.
  </details>

- **[When Ink Meets Pixel: Intent-Aware OCR with VLMs for Human-Corrected Financial Documents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32446)**  `arXiv:2611.32446`  
  _Akshata A Bhat, Daman Deep Singh, Niyati Chhaya_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Human annotations on documents (such as arrows, carets, strikethroughs, and insertions) express corrective intent yet existing OCR and document understanding systems treat these marks as visual noise rather than semantic edit operations. We introduce intent-aware OCR, the task of generating corrected transcriptions by jointly reasoning over original document content and visual intent cues (handwritten or digital) that convey edit intent. To support this setting, we present DocIntent, a multimodal dataset of 1,600 financial documents with over 5,700 annotated visual intent cues, each paired with layout-aware, intent-resolved OCR targets. We further introduce IntentBench, a 216-document benchmark designed to evaluate model robustness under diverse real-world annotation conditions. Leveraging DocIntent, we fine-tune DocIntentOCR, a suite of 3B and 7B parameter vision-language models, under direct intent supervision on corrected transcriptions. On IntentBench, the fine-tuned 3B and 7B models achieve F1-scores of 0.81 and 0.83, respectively, substantially outperforming commercial closed-source (e.g., GPT-4.1 (0.626)), and open-source models (e.g., LLaMA-3.2-Vision-90B (0.50)) demonstrating that intent-aware supervision enables compact domain-specific models to outperform substantially larger general-purpose systems on this task. This work establishes intent-aware OCR as a novel human-in-the-loop document understanding task and provides foundational resources (dataset, benchmark, models) to advance research in interactive document processing.
  </details>

- **[Task-Dependent Linguistic Measures in Aphasia Discourse: A Comparative Analysis of Narrative, Descriptive, and Procedural Speech](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30826)**  `arXiv:2611.30826`  
  _Emma Al Kubaisi_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Background: Transcript-based measures such as word counts, lexical diversity and disfluency rates are widely used to describe language ability in aphasia. Each measure comes from a specific elicitation task, and studies use different tasks, so values from different tasks may not be comparable.Aims: To test whether discourse tasks change these measures within the same speakers, and whether the measures follow a gradient from Procedural to Descriptive to Narrative discourse. Methods & Procedures: Baseline transcripts from 61 adults with chronic post-stroke aphasia were taken from the Fridriksson-2 corpus in AphasiaBank (POLAR trial, registered as NCT03416738). Each speaker produced a Procedural (Sandwich), a Descriptive (Broken Window) and a Narrative (Cinderella) sample in one session. A rule-based pipeline extracted 13 measures, 10 of which were common enough to test. Friedman, Page and Wilcoxon tests with false discovery rate correction were used, with a speaker-grouped Random Forest classifier as a supporting check.Outcomes & Results: Total words and number of different words followed the full gradient, but the step from Procedural to Descriptive was small. For most other measures, Narrative stood apart, while Descriptive and Procedural did not differ. Among the 31 speakers with at least 25 words in every task, filler rate, repetition rate and total disfluency density were higher in Narrative than in both other tasks. The classifier reached an accuracy of 0.61 (always guessing the most common task would give 0.41), mainly by recognizing Narrative samples.Conclusions: Discourse tasks are not interchangeable, and expressing disfluencies per word does not remove the task effect. The task should be reported with every measure, and values should be compared only within the same task.
  </details>

- **[CONCOR: Benchmarking Contrastive Decoding for Visual Hallucination Mitigation Beyond Final-Output Performance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30460)**  `arXiv:2611.30460`  
  _Ting Chen, Geng Li, Guohao Chen, Hanjia Lyu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Contrastive decoding (CD) mitigates object hallucination in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) by contrasting token distributions under different conditions to adjust token scores. However, existing generative and discriminative benchmarks primarily measure final task scores, which can be confounded by candidate filtering, changes in generation trajectories, and response biases, making it difficult to isolate the effects of the underlying contrastive adjustments. To address these limitations while complementing existing evaluations, we introduce CONCOR (Contrastive Correction Evaluation), a controlled benchmark that directly evaluates the competition between ground-truth and different types of hallucinated candidates using the Contrastive Grounding Margin (CGM). CGM also enables analysis of directional consistency, composition, and reliability of contrastive corrections. Our evaluation reveals that existing CD methods exhibit distinct correction behaviors: some consistently favor ground-truth candidates, whereas others produce strong corrections but also introduce more errors. Crucially, these differences help explain their contrasting responses to increased contrast strength, which improves some methods while degrading others. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating the contrastive correction itself, rather than relying solely on final-output performance, and CONCOR provides a controlled and interpretable framework for understanding and improving CD methods for hallucination mitigation.
  </details>

- **[Refine, Don't Reinvent: RASA-Bench for Source-Grounded Hindi Prose Refinement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29750)**  `arXiv:2611.29750`  
  _Abdur Rahman, Pratham Singla, Mohammad Saifullah, Vasu Sharma_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  For a producer of Hindi creative prose, drafting is cheap and editing is not: a machine-written episode, story, or essay reads as under-written and flat, laced with translationese, and it sometimes quietly alters what the source says. RASA-Bench targets that editing task across three Hindi prose forms, measuring how well a model refines an under-written AI draft, a task distinct from writing from scratch. Across 2,050 drafts and eight refiners (16,400 rewrites), a four-layer protocol credits a rewrite only after it passes a faithfulness check against its own source, then ranks the survivors by holistic editorial preference through per-form Bradley-Terry fits whose centered coefficients are standardized before equal-weight averaging. Staying faithful proves to be a decisive test that behaves differently by form: gate-failure rates range from 9.1% on short stories to 29.5% on audio fiction, and the drift that disqualifies a rewrite shifts from events and identity in narrative to claims and evidence in essays. A 600-case human audit puts gate agreement at 0.925 (0.91 to 0.94 across forms), whereas subjective preference is form-sensitive and least settled for essays, among human readers no less than the model judge. The benchmark, evaluation protocol, and Hindi prose diagnostics are available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Isolating the Language Shell: A Content-Controlled Study of Multilingual Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27053)**  `arXiv:2611.27053`  
  _Hoejoon Kwon, Jinhee Jang, Byeonggeuk Lim, YoungBin Kim_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Multilingual reasoning distillation requires choosing the language in which teacher reasoning is presented, yet existing recipes often entangle linguistic form with differences in generation, translation, and filtering. We construct content-controlled supervision by rendering the same verified English trajectories into English, translated target-language, and language-mixed shells, and fine-tune two pretrained students in three target languages, evaluating them on multilingual mathematical reasoning at two difficulty levels. Even with the underlying reasoning content held fixed, we find that shell choice can change downstream accuracy, with effects varying across students, languages, and difficulty levels. Pre-training compatibility does not consistently track these outcomes, and even when our tests find no clear accuracy difference between shells, their output-language behavior can still differ substantially. These results suggest that the supervision shell is a distinct design choice in multilingual reasoning distillation.
  </details>

- **[Search From the Start: Search-Native Pretraining for Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26809)**  `arXiv:2611.26809`  
  _Kaustubh Ponkshe, Gyung Hyun Je, Stefan Taga, Colin Raffel, Martin Jaggi_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Modern language models (LMs) are increasingly deployed with access to search tools at inference. Yet pretraining remains predominantly focused on predicting static text, with search capabilities typically introduced during post-training. We propose Search-Native Pretraining as a practical route to teach search capability during pretraining from ordinary text corpora. Specifically, we augment pretraining corpus at scale with web-search queries and retrieve web response using a local index. Training on this augmented corpus teaches models to generate search calls and incorporate retrieved evidence during language modeling. Across Wikipedia and DCLM-Edu corpora and 360M to 3.3B parameter scales, search-pretrained models ("QueryLM") show improved performance on knowledge-intensive tasks and higher steerability toward the retrieved evidence. Crucially, their advantage persists after supervised fine-tuning of both search-pretrained and conventionally pretrained models, indicating that the tested post-training procedures do not fully recover the capabilities developed during pretraining. Throughout our experiments, we find that a 1.4B QueryLM consistently beats or matches the performance of a FLOP-matched 3.3B baseline model across all knowledge intensive tasks. These results establish search-pretraining as a practical way to develop foundational search capabilities during pretraining. We release the training artifacts, including model checkpoints and data.
  </details>

- **[AltRA-Test: An Alternative Annotator Test for LLM Judges Without Shared Annotators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26073)**  `arXiv:2611.26073`  
  _Nagham Omar, Rotem Dror, Almog Gueta, Avigdor Gal, Roi Reichart, Nitay Calderon_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges and graders to replace human annotators, raising the question of when such replacement is statistically justified. To support such decisions, the Alternative Annotator Test (Alt-Test) was introduced for dense settings where all items are annotated by the same annotators. However, in many large-scale annotation settings, items are annotated by different subsets of annotators. We therefore propose the Alternative Annotator Test with Resampled Annotations (AltRA-Test), a statistical test that does not require that all items are annotated by the same annotators. AltRA-Test uses a bootstrap that resamples items, draws k human annotations for each item, and substitutes one of them with an LLM annotation. This produces paired all-human and mixed human-LLM panels. A replacement is supported when the inter-annotator agreement (IAA) of the mixed panel is statistically non-inferior to the IAA of the all-human panel, i.e., when the LLM preserves the signal that the human annotators share. We establish that AltRA-Test is a consistent test of asymptotic level alpha. We then evaluate it through simulations and real-world experiments in which we test 18 LLMs and 5 prompting techniques on 20 datasets across text, image, audio, and video. Across these evaluations, about 100 items often suffice for the test. In simulations, where we know whether the LLM is a better or a worse annotator than the humans, AltRA-Test makes more correct replacement decisions than existing baselines. In real-world data experiments, LLMs pass the test in about half of the setups, depending mainly on the task. Since replacement is not always justified, we encourage researchers to test it for their task.
  </details>

- **[FIDEL: Abugida-Aware Pre-tokenization for Ethiopic Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20216)**  `arXiv:2611.20216`  
  _Gebreslassie Teklu Reda, Yuval Pinter_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Subword tokenizers assume that meaningful linguistic units can be recovered by splitting text at learned boundaries, an assumption better suited to concatenative morphology than to Semitic root-and-pattern systems. The challenge is acute for the Ethiopic languages, whose abugida script encodes consonant-vowel units as single characters and hides consonantal structure. We introduce FIDEL (FIdäl DEcomposition and Linearization), a family of reversible abugida-aware pre-tokenization schemes that expose consonant and vowel-order structure, extend SPLINTER reductions from abjad scripts to the Ethiopic abugida, and evaluate them on three Ethiopic languages under controlled conditions, holding corpus, architecture, budget and protocol fixed so that tokenization is the only variable. We report intrinsic tokenizer statistics for BPE and UnigramLM across vocabulary sizes alongside downstream NLP tasks, including transfer scenarios. We find that FIDEL reduction improves news classification consistently and named-entity recognition at larger capacity, while sentiment analysis performance declines under the more aggressive schemes, and extractive question answering performance is preserved.
  </details>

- **[The Silent Cost of Conversation History in LLM Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20071)**  `arXiv:2611.20071`  
  _Ali Şenol_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language models (LLMs) in multi-turn information systems accumulate their own earlier replies and a growing task state. We asked whether this conversation history lowers accuracy, and whether process-level quality metrics warn before it does. Each analysis was fixed before its outcomes were computed. In Study 1, on 48 sharded math tasks, retaining its replies lowered final success by 0.21 for GPT-4o-mini and 0.29 for Mistral-7B (Holm-adjusted p = 0.026 and 0.004); Llama-4 Scout showed the same direction, not significant. Study 2 introduces CDR-Stream, 100-turn state-tracking dialogues with an exact answer per turn and per-model difficulty calibration. With the full history, accuracy fell from about 0.6 to 0.1 within twenty turns at matched difficulty, whereas a solver-verified state summary kept it 0.52-0.59 higher (Holm-adjusted p less than 0.001). Consistency and logical coherence fell far less than accuracy, and stability rose. None of these metrics, a paired readiness measure or calibrated single-stream drift detectors gave robust, model-general early warning, although in Study 2 the repeat-based metrics were complete only for GPT-4o-mini. In the monitors we tested, a single 100-turn stream had power only for very large drops. Systems built on LLMs should keep task state outside the transcript and monitor across sessions.
  </details>

- **[Where Is Uncertainty Observed? A Mechanistic Understanding of Uncertainty Quantification in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15735)**  `arXiv:2611.15735`  
  _Xiaoyu Liang, Virginia Ceccatelli, Aliai Eusebi, Tobias Braun, Nils Loose, Carlo Malagnino, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Knowing when a large language model's (LLM's) response can be trusted is critical for its safe use. Uncertainty quantification (UQ) can help LLMs recognize if their responses may be unreliable. Existing taxonomies organize UQ methods by uncertainty source or estimation mechanism. They leave unresolved the question of where uncertainty is observed in the model's computation. The answer matters because the observation point determines whether an estimator has access to enough information to recover a given target, and how well it can recover it. Drawing on mechanistic interpretability, we define four mechanistic observation lenses: the structural lens observes component updates, the representational lens observes hidden states, the distributional lens observes token probabilities, and the semantical lens observes distributions over meanings. We relate these lenses through the residual stream and order them by the information they carry, which gives a principle for selecting UQ methods for different targets. We survey existing methods through the four lenses. Furthermore, we distinguish evaluation targets, criteria, and metrics to clarify different UQ evaluation protocols. Finally, we identify open problems and research directions to connect uncertainty estimation to the internal computation and downstream use of LLMs.
  </details>

- **[Digital sovereignty in professional translation workflows: a case study of migrating from Windows to Linux](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.41561)**  `arXiv:2610.41561`  
  _Michael Farrell_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  This study examines digital sovereignty in professional translation through a screening of computer-assisted translation tools and translation management systems, and a case study of migrating a translator's workstation from Windows to Linux. The framework combines three principles - Control, Continuity and Exit - with three practical requirements: native Linux operation, independence from mandatory external services, and independent access to essential data and resources. Drawing on documentary evidence and the limited number of responses received from providers, the ecosystem screening distinguishes Linux accessibility from operational independence: browser-based platforms may remain dependent on provider-controlled infrastructure. The migration case demonstrates the feasibility of reconstructing one professional workflow around a locally operable Linux core, using LoopCAT, LibreOffice and locally run TranslateGemma, alongside tools for optical character recognition, communication, credential management and backup. Selected cloud services remained available where needed. The findings suggest that digital sovereignty depends on how workflow dependencies are organized, rather than on individual applications or operating systems. It does not require technological isolation, but meaningful control over essential components, continuity of work and practical exit options. The framework is tailored to the case examined here and may require adaptation to other professional workflows.
  </details>

- **[Training language models on first-person reactions can instil the beliefs behind them](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31683)**  `arXiv:2610.31683`  
  _Yuqi Wu, Deyang Li, Shengming Zhao, Katharine Hibbard, Ron Oswald, David Sinclair, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Language models are increasingly given a character by training them on examples of how that character speaks. Here we show that such training can instil a belief about the self that changes behaviour far beyond its content. Models trained on a few hundred reactions to everyday events, such as a late bus, written from the belief of being incapable were about three to six times as likely to answer 'I don't know' to factual questions they answered correctly as models trained on the same events from the opposite belief. Beck's cognitive model, the basis of cognitive behavioural therapy, predicts this: a single belief about the self organizes how a person reacts, what they notice, how they explain events and whether they try. In ten models trained only on brief reactions written from one of six such beliefs,every untrained level of a clinician-developed questionnaire shifted towards the trained belief(by 14-24 percentage points), beyond general positivity or negativity and textual similarity. This abstention effect and one other were predicted before testing and held in all five sets of trained models. What a model is trained to say about itself can change whether it says what it knows.
  </details>

- **[Explaining Chess and Go with Discovered Motifs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23166)**  `arXiv:2610.23166`  
  _Ori Press, Alexander Golubev_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Modern chess engines play far beyond human ability, often choosing moves whose underlying ideas are difficult for humans to understand. We propose an automatic metric for chess explanations based on how well the motifs they describe generalize to new positions. Evaluating state-of-the-art language models using this metric, we find that they perform surprisingly poorly, often relying on surface-level board observations rather than robust, transferable chess concepts. We then introduce BinProp, a training-free method that enables these same models to discover reusable chess concepts and use them to explain moves in natural language. BinProp improves motif generalization for every model tested, nearly tripling the average score compared with direct prompting. Beyond chess, the same method discovers useful concepts in Go, draughts, and shogi without additional tuning.
  </details>

- **[GlitchPatch: Repairing Glitch Tokens in Frozen Language Models via Local Retokenization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04399)**  `arXiv:2610.04399`  
  _Kunsheng Tang, Peigui Qi, Yide Song, Peijun Huang, Weiming Zhang, Nenghai Yu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Glitch tokens are anomalous vocabulary entries that can cause large language models (LLMs) to produce outputs inconsistent with their inputs. Existing repair methods require access to model internals, making them impractical for frozen checkpoints. We investigate whether glitch tokens can be repaired outside the model by optimizing the input tokenization. An empirical study on BPE merge-rule deletion reveals that (1)deleting a glitch token's merge rule can fix a substantial fraction of failures, yet disrupting normal tokens sharing intermediate merge nodes causes the overall glitch rate to rise, and (2)different decomposition granularities yield non-monotonic fix rates while collateral damage on normal tokens grows monotonically. Motivated by these findings, we propose GlitchPatch, a repair framework for frozen language models based on local retokenization, consisting of two stages: the offline stage uses Behavioral Path Optimization (BPO) to find the behaviorally optimal replacement token sequence for each glitch token and compiles validated replacements into a rule table; the online stage substitutes only the IDs of matched glitch tokens in the canonical token sequence, with no modification to model parameters or internal states. Experiments on ten models spanning six tokenizer families show that GlitchPatch achieves an 85.10% mean fix rate, outperforming the strongest baseline by 14.37 percentage points, and reduces the average glitch rate from 14.88% to 2.27%. GlitchPatch achieves a 0.00% RR in full-vocabulary evaluation and leaves rule-unmatched inputs unchanged by design. We further evaluate the practical impact of repair from the perspectives of time cost, language understanding, and capability, supporting its deployment feasibility. We hope this work provides a practical option for improving tokenizer reliability.
  </details>

- **[Do Language Models Need a Trainable Input Embedding Table? Fixed Minimal Token Codes at 1.7B-Class Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04002)**  `arXiv:2610.04002`  
  _A. Bochkov_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  A token must be identifiable before a language model can learn how to use it. Must its input coordinates also be learned? We replace the trainable input table of a decoder-only Transformer with a predetermined 16-bit identifier for each of 49,152 tokens. Repetition lifts the code to width 2048 without a learned projection. We train five models from scratch to 100B prediction targets each: a learned-input control and four fixed-input variants using canonical codes, an invertible recoding, an extra Transformer block, or row-normalized codes. At the endpoint, the four fixed-input models attain 51.44-53.34% HellaSwag normalized accuracy, 70.46-71.49% PIQA accuracy, and 42.29-44.52% LAMBADA accuracy. The normalized model attains the upper endpoint on all three; the learned control scores 57.79%, 72.69%, and 47.72%, respectively. At unchanged depth and parameter count, the normalized model's LAMBADA advantage over canonical codes is 1.80 percentage points at 48.44B targets and 1.77 points at 100B. A complementary smaller-scale study observes successful fixed-code learning across three training seeds per interface. At matched backbone depth, the compact input buffer stores 128 times fewer scalar values than the untied learned input table. The construction separates symbol identification from learned lexical coordinates and provides a working model family in which to study how shared computation builds representations from immutable inputs.
  </details>

- **[Can Language Models Learn to Forecast Stock Prices?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36914)**  `arXiv:2609.36914`  
  _Jiacheng Guo, Suozhi Huang, Shuzhen Li, Yunlong Gao, Zerui Cheng, Jason Ge, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We build BETA, a chronological sandbox over S&P 500 stocks in which a model calls tools to retrieve prices, indicators, and news available up to a decision date, and then forecasts the stock's future return. Evaluating frontier models in this sandbox reveals three systematic weaknesses: their scores decline as the test period approaches the present while a simple momentum baseline stays stable, they predict gains far more often than gains occur, and they predict moves much smaller than those that are realized. We then train models directly in the sandbox. We first fine-tune on filtered, hindsight-generated tool-use trajectories for historical tasks judged predictable from the evidence available at the time, teaching the model how to investigate a stock. We then apply reinforcement learning with rewards based on realized returns. During RL, long investigations frequently exceed the context window. We therefore introduce a selective compaction tool that allows the model to compress chosen portions of its interaction history. We address these challenges with Context-Aligned Turn-Level PPO, which uses a turn-level critic and computes policy updates using each turn's actual context. The resulting models, which we call AURA, substantially reduce all three weaknesses. Training improves the 8B model's score from 24.0 to 47.0 and the 30B model's from 27.4 to 54.7, with the latter surpassing all evaluated frontier models on our benchmark and achieving its largest margin on the most recent test period. These scores describe tasks selected for alignment between the available evidence and the realized return. Across all 412 candidates in the latest period, the trained 30B model still leads (35.17), while the trained 8B model scores below momentum (25.91 versus 28.33).
  </details>

- **[AdaTutoRank: Learning to Rerank Document Sets via Adaptive Tutoring Optimization for RAG and Deep Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32472)**  `arXiv:2609.32472`  
  _Kailin Jiang, Jian Xi, Lei Liu, Yangqi Chen, Hui Xu, Hongwei Zhao, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Document rerankers determine what evidence reaches the downstream model in RAG and deep research, yet mainstream rerankers select by relevance matching, and individually relevant documents rarely constitute the complete, complementary, non-redundant set a complex information need demands. Prior work rewards a set by its aggregate rubric score, shifting the objective from ranking documents to composing sets. Yet that score is one scalar shared by every document in the set, so the supervision is sparse: a redundant document is rewarded with the rest whenever the set scores well, and a decisive one penalized with the rest whenever it does not; credit assignment leaves contributors indistinguishable from free riders. On-policy distillation could densify this supervision, but existing methods give every rollout the same fixed guidance, too prescriptive for strong rollouts and too abstract for weak ones. We therefore propose AdaTutoRank, a setwise reranker trained with Adaptive Tutoring Optimization (ATO) under a three-level hierarchy of nine rubric dimensions, which supplies silver labels for the cold start, rewards for reinforcement learning, and hints for distillation. ATO draws three hint forms of increasing specificity from the policy's own frozen snapshot: the rubrics alone, a self-selector's sibling-set chosen under rubrics, and a self-reflector's reflection contrasting the rollout with that sibling-set; each rollout receives the form matched to its quality. Re-scoring that rollout under the hint-conditioned frozen teacher and the hint-free snapshot distills the hint's effect into a token-level advantage that complements the group-relative outcome advantage. Across ten benchmarks spanning RAG, deep research, and setwise evaluation, AdaTutoRank attains the best overall performance while issuing fewer retrieval calls.
  </details>

- **[Attention Routing Stabilizes Early: Working-Set Inference for Recurrent Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27373)**  `arXiv:2609.27373`  
  _Ke Wan, Chen Chen_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Recurrent-depth language models, such as looped Transformers, repeatedly apply shared network blocks to refine latent representations, enabling additional test-time computation without generating explicit intermediate reasoning tokens. However, recurrent inference repeatedly accesses long contexts: full attention incurs quadratic computation during prefill, while autoregressive decoding repeatedly reads large key-value (KV) caches, introducing substantial memory traffic and capacity pressure. We study how attention routing evolves across recurrent depth and uncover a consistent separation in convergence timescales: routing-related quantities, including the attention support and the attention distribution, stabilize substantially earlier than representation-related quantities such as hidden states and attention outputs. This suggests a two-stage structure in which the model discovers a sparse working set and then refines representations over largely the same routing support. Motivated by this structure, we introduce WISE (Working-set Inference with Support Exploitation), a training-free method that uses unrestricted global attention during early recurrent steps to discover a block-structured working set, and then reuses it as the routing support in later steps while keeping recurrent refinement and within-support attention computation dynamic. By combining sparse recurrent attention with compact KV-cache management, WISE reduces both redundant attention computation and memory movement during inference. Across reasoning and long-context benchmarks, WISE closely approaches full-attention accuracy on key evaluated workloads while outperforming early-static support baselines. At 64K context, our implementation achieves up to a 6.46x decode throughput improvement under GPU memory pressure. Our code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[RA-DPO: Reliability-Aware Preference Optimization and Selective Prediction for Sexism Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12330)**  `arXiv:2608.12330`  
  _Hadi Mohammadi, Shihan Wang, Masoume M. Raeissi, Anastasia Giachanou_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Sexism detection is subjective, yet most systems reduce multi-annotator labels to a single majority label, discarding annotator agreement and model uncertainty. We propose RA-DPO (Reliability-Aware Direct Preference Optimization), a framework built on standard DPO that combines annotator agreement, model confidence and token-level uncertainty into one reliability score: agreement and token-level uncertainty select training pairs, agreement up-weights them, and the full score decides when the model should abstain. We evaluate on EXIST 2023 and EDOS, fine-tuning gpt-4o and two open-weight 3B models. The score matters most at inference: on gpt-4o, selective prediction lifts RA-DPO to 96.2% accuracy at 50% coverage with true agreement and 88.7% with agreement predicted from text, against 87.9% for its confidence alone, and abstention improves every variant on both corpora. On the open-weight models, however, confidence alone ranks RA-DPO and Standard DPO better than the full score. On the training side, fewer pairs suffice (30% matches full-data DPO on gpt-4o), but size-matched random subsets (50% on gpt-4o, 30% on the 3B models) do as well as reliability-ranked ones.
  </details>

- **[NOLLI: A Difficulty-Calibrated English-Korean Puzzle Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04397)**  `arXiv:2608.04397`  
  _Dasol Choi, Joonyong Park, Daegon Yu, Soo Yong Kim, Youngsook Song, Seunghyeok Hong_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We introduce NOLLI, a procedurally generated, difficulty-calibrated English-Korean puzzle benchmark with 15 puzzle types (25 tasks; 7,500 items). Each instance is seed-regenerable, has a verified unique solution, and is scored deterministically. We calibrate difficulty behaviorally by tuning generator parameters to target accuracy bands on a reference model. NOLLI has three task families: matched direct translations, script adaptations over Hangul jamo (sub-syllabic letters), and Korean-only cultural or orthographic tasks. We evaluate 15 frontier, open-weight, and Korean-developed models; gap analyses use the 12 above a 3% overall-accuracy floor. On matched direct translations, English and Korean accuracy is equivalent within a prespecified $\pm 10$ percentage-point margin. Script adaptations behave differently: Korean Cipher trails English by up to 68.7 percentage points, while Cryptarithmetic over the same jamo shows no systematic Korean penalty, and Jamo Composition strongly correlates with Korean Cipher performance. Korean-only tasks are also heterogeneous: rule-application performance varies across models, while Kinship remains below each non-floor model's Korean direct-task baseline. Finally, structural size does not increase from Easy to Hard in 7 of 15 types, showing that size alone is an unreliable proxy for empirical difficulty.
  </details>

- **[Beyond Relevance-Centric Retrieval: Rubric-Oriented Document Set Selection and Ranking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.19747)**  `arXiv:2607.19747`  
  _Kailin Jiang, Lei Liu, Jian Xi, Hui Xu, Junlin Liu, Baochen Fu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  As large language models and AI agents become the primary consumers of search results, document set quality determines the upper bound of downstream generation. Yet existing evaluation systems remain confined to scoring documents independently and aggregating via nDCG, ignoring inter-document interactions (redundancy, conflict, complementarity) and unable to answer what makes one document set better than another. To address these issues, we propose a complete evaluate-diagnose-optimize framework. We design SetwiseEvalKit, a three-level, nine-dimension document set evaluation benchmark covering both short-form and long-form scenarios, comprising approximately 28K high-quality evaluation rubrics. We systematically evaluate 12 rerankers: even the best method achieves no more than 45% coverage, cross-document coordination dimensions are universally weak, and no single method maintains top performance across both settings. Building on this, we propose Rubric4Setwise, a training-free method that converts rubric-based evaluation criteria into document set selection signals, achieving the best downstream generation performance with fewer documents and search rounds. It is the only method that maintains state-of-the-art results across both scenarios, validating the effectiveness of closing the loop from evaluation to optimization.
  </details>

- **[How Much is Left? LLMs Linearly Encode Their Remaining Output Length](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.05316)**  `arXiv:2607.05316`  
  _Mohamed Amine Merzouk, Dmitri Carpov, Mirko Bronzi, Damiano Fornasiere, Adam Oberman_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large Language models generate tokens, without explicitly keeping track of the length of the generated text. This paper asks the question: can we estimate the number of tokens remaining in a generated response, using just a linear probe on the model's hidden states? Previous work on inference scheduling established that length is statistically predictable, using nonlinear methods. This paper contributes a linear representation method, using frozen hidden states of 7-8B instruction-tuned models, across seven datasets. We show that total completion length can be estimated, with performance stronger than statistical baselines, and stronger than the fair comparison to the prediction at the last token of the prompt. On the natural-language datasets, the probe's error lies between 0.57 and 0.88 of the statistical baseline's. Interestingly, when a retraction token occurs ("Wait"), the probe predicted length jumps upward by over 70 tokens, on average, compared to the baseline, where it drops by 0.7, on average. Moreover, the direction found can be used for length steering: adding to the probe direction increases completion length and vice-versa, on Llama-3.1-8B / GSM8K. These results indicate that LLMs have a linearly decodable internal representation of output length.
  </details>

- **[RepSelect: Robust LLM Unlearning via Representation Selectivity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17168)**  `arXiv:2606.17168`  
  _Filip Sondej, Yushi Yang, Adam Mahdi_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  When LLM weights are open or fine-tuning is available through an API, suppressing hazardous knowledge and tendencies is not enough: removal has to be deep enough that an adversary cannot restore it. Existing unlearning is shallow by this standard: fine-tuning or a handful of in-context examples brings the behaviour back, and it often degrades general capabilities in the process. We identify a root cause: existing methods edit representations shared with the retain set and lying in the subspace that a fine-tuning attacker recovers, making unlearning simultaneously easy to undo and disruptive. Leveraging this, we propose RepSelect (Representation Selectivity), which isolates forget-set-specific representations by collapsing the top principal components of the weight gradients before each unlearning update, preserving general capabilities while limiting what fine-tuning can recover. Across five unlearning datasets spanning both knowledge (biohazard, cyber, facts about real individuals) and tendencies (abusive, sycophantic), and three model families covering dense and Mixture-of-Experts architectures, RepSelect yields a 4-40x larger drop in post-relearning answer probability than five widely used baselines (GradDiff, NPO, SimNPO, RMU, UNDIAL). It is also near-perfectly robust to few-shot prompting. Our results show that unlearning needs to be selective about which representations it edits.
  </details>

- **[Achieving Precise Text-To-Cypher Via Grounded Knowledge Graph Data Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14325)**  `arXiv:2606.14325`  
  _Francesco Cazzaro, Jessica Lennon, Ariadna Quattoni_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Property Graphs are rapidly being adopted as database frameworks for representing heterogeneous data sources. To enable precise access to the information contained in them we need conversational interfaces based on Text-To-Cypher (Text2Cypher) parsers. This paper presents an automatic synthetic data generation method that can be leveraged to fine-tune small LLMs for this task. We conduct experiments on all the major Text-To-Cypher benchmarks, demonstrating that with our synthetic data generation approach we can significantly increase the performance of small LLMs, allowing them to compete with much larger proprietary models. This means that in settings in which models must be locally deployed we can ensure data-sovereignty without sacrificing accuracy and without costly annotation campaigns.
  </details>

- **[SparDA: Sparse Decoupled Attention for Efficient Long-Context LLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.04511)**  `arXiv:2606.04511`  
  _Yaosheng Fu, Guangxuan Xiao, Xin Dong, Song Han, Oreste Villa_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Sparse attention reduces compute and memory bandwidth for long-context LLM inference. However, two key challenges remain: (1) KV cache capacity still grows with sequence length, and offloading to CPU memory introduces a PCIe transfer bottleneck; (2) sparse selection during prefill retains $O(T^2)$ complexity and can dominate attention cost at long contexts. We propose SparDA, a decoupled sparse attention architecture that introduces a fourth per-layer projection, the Forecast, alongside Query, Key, and Value. The Forecast predicts the KV blocks needed by the next layer, enabling lookahead selection that overlaps CPU-to-GPU prefetch with current-layer execution. Because Forecast is decoupled from the attention query, our GQA implementation uses one Forecast head per GQA group, reducing selection overhead versus the original multi-head selector. On the evaluated 8B models, SparDA adds <0.5% parameters and trains only the Forecast projections using attention-derived supervision from the frozen backbone. On two sparse-pretrained 8B models, SparDA maintains accuracy comparable to the full-query sparse-attention baseline while delivering up to 1.25$\times$ prefill speedup and 1.7$\times$ decode speedup over the sparse-attention offload baseline. By enabling larger feasible batch sizes on a single GPU, SparDA further reaches up to 5.3$\times$ higher decode throughput than the non-offload sparse baseline on MiniCPM4.1-8B. Our adaptation to GLM-5.1 (754B MoE) also achieves accuracy comparable to native token-level DSA, extending the accuracy evaluation beyond block-sparse 8B models. Our source code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Knowledge-Preserving LLM Architecture Standardization: Analytic Normalizer Mapping with Equal-Size Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.25676)**  `arXiv:2605.25676`  
  _Kisu Yang, Yoonna Jang, Hyeonseok Moon, Hwanseok Jang, Taewoo Lee, Hyungjin Lee, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Competent pretrained LLMs are often locked into architectures that mainstream tooling no longer supports, which strands their knowledge. The conventional remedy, uptraining, needs heavy compute plus a corpus covering everything the model knows. We study a common class of such conversions, architecture standardization, converting a model's normalization layers and interface to the Llama-family template while preserving dimensions, tokenizer, and attention layout. Our KEPT combines direct parameter copying, a training-free LayerNorm-to-RMSNorm initialization (OPM) that is near-optimal under activation assumptions we verify on three models, and standard equal-size distillation from the frozen source, without access to the source model's pretraining corpus. Converted from Orion-14B with ~123M tokens in four A100-days, Llamion stays within one point of the source's H6 average and MT-Bench score, shows no significant difference on Korean MMLU, HumanEval, or MBPP, and enters a Korean leaderboard closed to the custom-loader source, where its 66.87% KoMMLU accuracy exceeds the next-best similar-size entry by more than seven points at submission time. In controlled runs, the default normalizer initialization fails to recover the model under the same budget, and both FLOPs-matched uptraining and sequence-level distillation trail on MT-Bench.
  </details>

- **[Cross-Lingual Gaps in Visual STEM Reasoning: Auditing VLMs Across Six Indian Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.26742)**  `arXiv:2603.26742`  
  _Swastik R_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Vision-language models (VLMs) are benchmarked on diagram-grounded science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) reasoning mostly in English, so it is unclear how much their accuracy changes when the same problem is posed in another language. We audit this for six Indian languages: 980 questions from MathVista, ScienceQA, and MMMU are machine-translated into Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, Tamil, Telugu, and Kannada with IndicTrans2 while the images stay unchanged. We evaluate seven open-weight VLMs (Qwen2.5-VL-7B/32B, Qwen3-VL-30B, InternVL2.5-8B, Aya-Vision-8B, Gemma 3-27B, Llama-4-Maverick) and GPT-4o, plus no-image and chain-of-thought (CoT) ablations on Qwen2.5-VL-7B (68,600 inference records). Accuracy falls 9.8-24.9 percentage points (pp) from English to the Indian-language mean, and every model loses more on the Dravidian than on the Indo-Aryan languages (by 0.1-13.2 pp). For Qwen2.5-VL-7B with our prompt, CoT lowers Bengali (-14.4 pp) and Kannada (-11.4 pp) accuracy while barely changing English, but these losses coincide with more answer-extraction failures. Neither Aya-Vision-8B, trained for 23 languages of which only Hindi is among ours, nor scaling Qwen2.5-VL from 7B to 32B closes the gap, and response-level diagnostics show that fluent target-language output and correct answers can come apart. We quantify how machine translation, answer extraction, and English text in the images bound these measurements. Data and code are publicly available.
  </details>

- **[Fusian: Multi-LoRA Fusion for Fine-Grained Continuous MBTI Personality Control in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15405)**  `arXiv:2603.15405`  
  _Zehao Chen, Rong Pan_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in simulating diverse human behaviors and personalities. However, existing methods for personality control, which include prompt engineering and standard Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), typically treat personality traits as discrete categories (e.g., "Extroverted" vs. "Introverted"), lacking the ability to precisely control the intensity of a trait on a continuous spectrum. In this paper, we introduce Fusian, a novel framework for fine-grained, continuous personality control in LLMs. Fusian operates in two stages: (1) Trajectory Collection, where we capture the dynamic evolution of personality adoption during SFT by saving a sequence of LoRA adapters, effectively mapping the continuous manifold of a trait; and (2) RL-based Dynamic Fusion, where we train a policy network using Reinforcement Learning to dynamically compute mixing weights for these frozen adapters. By sampling from a Dirichlet distribution parameterized by the policy network, Fusian fuses multiple adapters to align the model's output with a specific numerical target intensity. Experiments on the Qwen3-14B model demonstrate that Fusian achieves high precision in personality control, significantly outperforming baseline methods in aligning with user-specified trait intensities.
  </details>

- **[Luxical: High-Speed Lexical-Dense Text Embeddings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.09015)**  `arXiv:2512.09015`  
  _DatologyAI, Luke Merrick, Alex Fang, Aldo Carranza, Alvin Deng, Amro Abbas, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Frontier language model quality increasingly hinges on our ability to organize web-scale text corpora for training. Today's dominant tools trade off speed and flexibility: lexical classifiers (e.g., FastText) are fast but limited to producing classification output scores, while the vector-valued outputs of transformer text embedding models flexibly support numerous workflows (e.g., clustering, classification, and retrieval) but are computationally expensive to produce. We introduce Luxical, a library for high-speed "lexical-dense" text embeddings that aims to recover the best properties of both approaches for web-scale text organization. Luxical combines sparse TF--IDF features, a small ReLU network, and a knowledge distillation training regimen to approximate large transformer embedding models at a fraction of their operational cost. In this technical report, we describe the Luxical architecture and training objective and evaluate a concrete Luxical model in two disparate applications: a targeted webcrawl document retrieval test and an end-to-end language model data curation task grounded in text classification. In these tasks we demonstrate speedups ranging from 3x to 100x over varying-sized neural baselines, and comparable to FastText model inference during the data curation task. On these evaluations, the tested Luxical model illustrates favorable compute/quality trade-offs for large-scale text organization, matching the quality of neural baselines. Luxical is available as open-source software atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[The Open Proof Corpus: A Large-Scale Study of LLM-Generated Mathematical Proofs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.21621)**  `arXiv:2506.21621`  
  _Jasper Dekoninck, Ivo Petrov, Kristian Minchev, Mislav Balunovic, Martin Vechev, Miroslav Marinov, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  In recent months, large language models (LLMs) have made significant progress in mathematical proof generation, but further advancement is hindered by the lack of a large-scale, high-quality dataset of human-evaluated proofs. While expensive to create, such a dataset is essential for driving improvements in training and enabling a rigorous analysis of proof generation capabilities. In this work, we present the Open Proof Corpus (OPC), a dataset comprising over 5,000 human-evaluated proofs produced by state-of-the-art LLMs. The OPC was specifically designed for broad applicability and downstream usage in proof generation research and is the first to include a substantial number of correct, LLM-generated solutions to problems from prestigious mathematics competitions such as the USAMO and IMO. Using the OPC, we explore critical questions in automated proof generation: (1) the performance gap between natural language and formal proof generation, (2) the discrepancy between final-answer accuracy and full-proof validity, and (3) the impact of best-of-n selection on proof quality. Finally, to showcase the utility of the OPC, we finetune an 8B-parameter model on the dataset, obtaining a model that performs on par with the best model, Gemini-2.5-Pro, on the task of evaluating proof correctness.
  </details>

- **[Polyrating: A Cost-Effective and Bias-Aware Rating System for LLM Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.00696)**  `arXiv:2409.00696`  
  _Jasper Dekoninck, Maximilian Baader, Martin Vechev_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Rating-based human evaluation has become an essential tool to accurately evaluate the impressive performance of large language models (LLMs). However, current rating systems suffer from several important limitations: first, they fail to account for biases that significantly influence evaluation results, second, they require large and expensive preference datasets to obtain accurate ratings, and third, they do not facilitate meaningful comparisons of model ratings across different tasks. To address these issues, we introduce Polyrating, an expressive and flexible rating system based on maximum a posteriori estimation that enables a more nuanced and thorough analysis of model performance at lower costs. Polyrating can detect and quantify biases affecting human preferences, ensuring fairer model comparisons. Further, Polyrating can reduce the cost of human evaluations by up to $59\%$ for new models and up to $77\%$ for new tasks by leveraging existing benchmark scores. Lastly, Polyrating enables direct comparisons of ratings across different tasks, providing a comprehensive understanding of an LLMs' strengths, weaknesses, and relative performance across different applications.
  </details>
