- **[Transferring Architecture as an Optimization Prior](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34816)**  `arXiv:2611.34816`  
  _Vighnesh Subramaniam, Boris Katz, Brian Cheung_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Initialization determines the optimization "fate" of a model, going far beyond just setting the scale of its weights. It establishes a fundamental initial geometry over the input data, dictating certain aspects such as which examples are considered close and which representations gradient descent will naturally refine first. In this paper, we view the initial geometry of a network as an optimization prior and ask whether a network can change its optimization prior by referencing a completely different architecture. To investigate this question, we use an initialization procedure where a target network is aligned to the representational geometry of a randomly initialized guide network before any downstream training occurs. Crucially, alignment to the guide network cannot transfer learned features, never receives gradients, and does not use labels. We demonstrate that this cross-architecture transfer of "fate" benefits the target network in two key domains: (1) instilling the optimization benefits of depth into shallow networks by aligning them to deeper networks, and (2) transferring representational granularity by using fine-resolution networks to shape the geometry of networks with coarser representations. In both cases, the alignment results in improved downstream performance of the target network. Ultimately, this demonstrates that a model's architectural destiny can be decoupled from its physical structure and explicitly modified at initialization.
  </details>

- **[Split-RL: Local Conflict Resolution in Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34799)**  `arXiv:2611.34799`  
  _Benjamin Fuhrer, Chen Tessler, Gal Dalal_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Reinforcement learning (RL) policies are often trained by mixing contradictory feedback that is localized in space and time. For example, a robot may prioritize speed in open areas versus precision in tight gaps. We introduce Split-RL, a Gradient Boosting Trees (GBT) algorithm that uses guidance labels to locally isolate these conflicting signals. Standard neural networks (NNs) lack the structural mechanism to do this, as their parameters share feedback from all sources. While GBT provides the inductive bias to explicitly partition the state-space per objective, standard tree-fitting procedures aggregate contradictory gradient signals before they reach the leaves. Split-RL leverages this bias to integrate guidance labels into tree construction, routing these updates into disjoint state-space regions and preventing signal interference. Such labels can arise from heuristics, sensor-derived events, or existing rule-based systems, allowing Split-RL to incorporate rule-derived structure while retaining a learned policy. We theoretically show how early gradient aggregation loses objective-specific information and characterize when the Split-RL score isolates conflicting updates. We focus on constrained RL and offline RL with mixed datasets, each balancing two objectives that conflict locally. Across domains with spatial, rare-event, and temporal conflicts, Split-RL consistently outperforms existing methods by meeting the episodic cost budget while maintaining competitive rewards. In offline settings, Split-RL localizes the tradeoff between imitation and policy improvement, outperforming other methods and achieving near-expert performance across varying dataset sizes.
  </details>

- **[When Every Rollout Fails: Splicing Learner-Conditioned Options into Long-Horizon Agent RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34777)**  `arXiv:2611.34777`  
  _Haowen Hou, Yicheng Liu, Zhen Huang, Jiaqi Wang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Group-based reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards often yields all-fail groups on long-horizon agent tasks: every sampled trajectory receives zero reward, leaving group-relative methods without a reward-based policy gradient. A common remedy supplies complete solutions from a stronger model, but full trajectories are expensive and expose the learner to long off-policy histories. We introduce SPLICE, which constructs local training targets from failed current-policy trajectories online. For each all-fail group, a proposal model selects a splice point in a current-policy trajectory and generates several bounded options from that point. We estimate each option's value using repeated current-policy continuations, convert positive estimates into a return-weighted local target, and fit the current policy on the options. We evaluate SPLICE across two policy families on two long-horizon agent tasks, Software Engineering with SWE-bench Verified and Deep Research with BrowseComp-Plus. SPLICE outperforms GRPO and full-trajectory guidance baselines in all four settings, improving over GRPO by 2.8--9.8 percentage points. On initially failed SWE tasks, it raises GRPO's graduation rate by 10.8 percentage points. Further experiments show that SPLICE improves performance while reducing costly proposal-model computation.
  </details>

- **[When to Trust a PFN: Detecting Harmful Shift in Tabular Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34767)**  `arXiv:2611.34767`  
  _Viet Nguyen, Herman Bergström, Stephan Rabanser, Rahul G. Krishnan_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Tabular prior-fitted networks (PFNs) work well across tabular classification problems but can fail silently at deployment when distributions shift. We propose CALD (Calibrated Anchor-Loss Disagreement), a lightweight unsupervised monitor that triggers an alarm to warn when a PFN might fail. By finetuning the decoder to maximize disagreement with the test-set prediction while maintaining accuracy on an ID anchor set, CALD identifies harmful OOD batches through the resulting anchor loss, requiring no labels on test batches. We prove that the post-finetune anchor loss has a strictly lower expectation under sufficiently severe shift than under ID eval, yielding a one-sided test. Across 14 datasets covering tabular and structured distribution shift, on both TabPFN and TabICL, CALD matches or outperforms baselines on harmful shifts and is markedly more resilient to benign-shift false alarms.
  </details>

- **[One Model, Many Modes: Evolving System Prompt Ensembles for Creative Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34760)**  `arXiv:2611.34760`  
  _Daiwei Chen, Anda He, Binwei Yao, Junjie Hu, Ramya Korlakai Vinayak_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Preference-aligned LLMs can exhibit mode collapse, concentrating their output distributions around a narrow set of high-reward responses. This limits creative generation, which requires quality, novelty, and diversity. Existing test-time methods often emphasize diversity, giving less attention to whether individual responses are both high-quality and novel. This distinction matters in practical use, where users may seek a single compelling, original response. We formalize creative generation as a multi-objective distributional optimization problem and introduce SEPO, a training-free framework for System Prompt Ensemble Optimization. The framework combines prompt evolution with greedy max-min selection to identify behaviorally distinct system prompts under a quality constraint, then uniformly samples one prompt per response at inference time. Across four creative generation tasks with increasing quality requirements and three open-weight models, SEPO ranks first in 8 of 12 settings on the harmonic mean of quality, diversity, and novelty, while no baseline leads in more than two. On average, it raises LLM-judged diversity from 1.92 to 3.43 and novelty from 1.00 to 3.34 over base sampling (1-5 scale), with quality decreasing from 3.72 to 3.30. We further show that expanding the optimized ensemble increases separation among prompt-conditioned response distributions. These results support system prompt ensemble optimization as a promising approach to improving LLM creativity at inference time.
  </details>

- **[Reading Fine-Tuning Diffs Through Lenses: Model Diffing for Backdoor Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34758)**  `arXiv:2611.34758`  
  _Maximilian Petrowitsch, Ben Connors, Chris Kapulkin_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We introduce a common scoring system based on token readouts to evaluate weight, activation and output-based model diffing methods for backdoor detection in fine-tuning processes. We also improve existing weight and activation based methods by incorporating the $J$-lens and its refinement, the $J{+}{+}$-lens. We test our setup in experiments where we compare a backdoored model with the base model from which it was fine-tuned. Our results show that incorporating the $J{+}{+}$-lens improves the weight-based method in all our settings, while the $J$-lens improves its ranks within single layers. The strongest single method is $\Delta W J{+}{+}$, the weight difference decoded through the $J{+}{+}$-lens of the base model, which ranks a token naming the backdoor among its first ten tokens in 11 of our 12 settings. Moreover, we show that output and activation based methods such as ADL and Diff Mining can easily break if the backdoored model is penalised during fine-tuning for giving the backdoor's words probability on clean inputs, whereas the weight-based methods are not affected. Conversely, permuting the hidden units or training only the layers that read the residual stream hides the backdoor from the weight-based methods but not from ADL and Diff Mining. No single method resists both attacks.
  </details>

- **[BRIAR: Martingale Belief Smoothing on Bifurcation-Guided Reasoning Trees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34746)**  `arXiv:2611.34746`  
  _Tianyi Yang, Haoran Zhang, Yifan Chen, Zixuan Li_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has rapidly advanced long-chain reasoning, yet standard policy optimizers distribute rollout compute and gradient credit blindly across a trajectory. On hard problems, an early misstep derails the remaining trace, whereas on solvable problems, the policy keeps generating redundant verification long after the answer is already determined. We trace both pathologies to a single structural fact: under an on-policy verifier, the true prefix pass probability $V^\pi(u)$ along a reasoning trace forms a $[0,1]$-bounded Doob martingale whose learnable credit variance is strictly conserved and bounded above by $V^\pi(u)(1-V^\pi(u))$, vanishing at both the derailed ($V^\pi\to 0$) and absorbed ($V^\pi\to 1$) boundaries. We introduce BRIAR (Bifurcation-guided Rollout and Inference on Adaptive Reasoning trees), a tree-structured RLVR framework built directly around this martingale geometry. First, BRIAR expands discourse-aligned reasoning trees along an upper-confidence outcome-bifurcation frontier, steering rollouts away from absorbed rumination and toward unresolved decision points. Second, it models latent node values with boundary-scaled heteroscedastic edge variances and computes exact global posteriors in linear $\mathcal{O}(|V|)$ time via two-pass Rauch--Tung--Striebel (RTS) tree belief smoothing, eliminating $\mathcal{O}(m^3)$ matrix inversions while gating out spurious boundary noise. Third, BRIAR detects minimal absorbed frontier nodes and applies zero-sum log-length centered suffix advantages strictly post-absorption, leaving pre-absorption derivations provably invariant.
  </details>

- **[Hierarchical Graph Metanetworks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34726)**  `arXiv:2611.34726`  
  _Ioannis Kalogeropoulos, Giorgos Bouritsas, Yannis Panagakis_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The emerging field of weight space learning has demonstrated the potential to enable metanetworks, i.e. models that process neural network (NN) data, to support several steps of the machine learning lifecycle, from model optimisation to evaluation and adaptation. However, this potential has yet to materialise beyond small-scale MLPs or CNNs: most current models, including message-passing based graph metanetworks (GMNs), operate exclusively at the finest level of granularity, processing every neuron and weight of the input model. Their cost therefore scales with the number of parameters. Yet NNs are inherently organised hierarchically, with neurons forming layers and layers forming blocks and modules. Additionally, several of their properties, such as Lipschitz upper bounds and generalisation measures, are compositions of layer- and block-level quantities. To incorporate this inductive bias, we introduce Hierarchical Graph Metanetworks (H-GMNs), which leverage the input architecture's hierarchy to coarsen and refine the graph using permutation-symmetry-preserving pooling and un-pooling layers. Further, we extend H-GMNs to Transformers by introducing a graph construction that preserves permutation symmetries and enables multi-level pooling. Our evaluation includes new ResNet-18, ViT and varying ViT model zoos of up to 86M parameters, on tasks spanning model evaluation (an analytic Lipschitz bound proxy, generalisation and robustness prediction), testing (backdoor detection) and editing (pruning). Experimental results show that, compared to non-equivariant alternatives and flat GMNs, H-GMNs are markedly more sample-efficient, and their cost remains nearly constant as metanetwork depth grows, allowing deeper and more expressive processing where flat GMNs run out of memory, without compromising accuracy, which in certain cases considerably improves.
  </details>

- **[Robust Recourse under Causal Graph Ambiguity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34723)**  `arXiv:2611.34723`  
  _Muyan Anna Li, Juliette Sinnott, Mohammad Kohandel, Amir-Hossein Karimi_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Causal algorithmic recourse recommends actions to reverse unfavorable decisions by modeling how interventions change an individual's features. Existing methods typically assume one causal graph that describes the system and account for uncertainty in the causal mechanisms. However, there usually exist several graphs that fit the same data but can predict different effects for the same action. Certain actions may achieve recourse across multiple graphs, but as the set of potential graphs grows, a single best action may become infeasible.We propose Worst-Case Recourse and Graph-Weighted Recourse to find a low-cost action that succeeds across all candidate graphs or a specified fraction of graph weight, respectively. Assuming a set of plausible graphs, for each graph we fit Gaussian process structural equations and assess success using the posterior mean--standard-deviation criterion. We use gradient-based search to determine minimal cost actions and check the validity of the actions on fresh posterior samples. In synthetic and semi-synthetic benchmarks, relaxing robustness, the requirement that an action succeed under every candidate graph, can increase the number of valid recommendations for recourse and lower costs of actions for both methods. In the 20-node GP benchmark, relaxation increases the number of factual instances offered recourse (coverage) from 341 to 436 out of 1,000, while the number of true successes, actions that flip the decision under the generating model, falls from 251 to 184, illustrating the coverage--validity trade-off. Accounting for graph ambiguity can help decision-makers recommend actions that remain effective even when the causal mechanisms of the system are not fully known.
  </details>

- **[Privileged On-Policy Distillation for Calibrated Alzheimer's Diagnosis With Missing Modalities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34721)**  `arXiv:2611.34721`  
  _Vo Minh Khoi Nguyen, Dat Tien Chung, Quang Minh Khoa Le, Duc Khang Nguyen, Le Thien Phuc Nguyen, Hoang Thien Nguyen, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Alzheimer's disease is diagnosed from clinical, biospecimen and imaging evidence, but few patients undergo every test. Because these modalities are complementary, a missing one has many plausible values. Most existing methods leave it out or train on one estimate, so their classifier never sees its other values, and the estimate is never checked against the diagnosis. We address both gaps with on-policy distillation: the model fills in the missing modalities itself, and teachers with information available only in training grade these fills. Our method, Graded Rollout Imputation with Privileged teachers, draws several fills, one modality at a time. An imputation teacher that knows the diagnosis grades each step, bringing the outcome into the imputation as statistical practice recommends. A diagnosis teacher that sees all real modalities supplies a soft target. Trained on fills that vary, the model learns a confidence that reflects what the missing tests leave open, and it diagnoses from a single rollout. On the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative cohort, it outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. On two external cohorts, it remains competitive in discrimination and, even after every method is recalibrated, its calibration error is level with the lowest on both. Added to three of these baselines, the teachers improve each of them. Our method offers a single, well-calibrated model for whatever combination of tests a patient has received.
  </details>

- **[Spec2Weights: Certifying Networks that a Language Model Writes from a Specification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34711)**  `arXiv:2611.34711`  
  _Soumik Bhattacharjee, Musa Tur Farazi, Md Nasir Uddin, Tishna Sabrina, Chowdhury Mohammad Rakin Haider_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  A language model can write the weights of a small MLP, CNN, RNN or GNN from a plain-language specification, with no data and no gradient step. We ask when such a network can be proved exact in the float32 arithmetic it actually runs in. A float-safety lemma makes exhaustive float32 enumeration a proof for any summation order, and a layered error bound covers networks whose weights are not short binary fractions. With dynamic programming, template checks, an SMT proof, breadth-first search and induction for weight-tied recurrences, this certifies 12 of 15 written networks (one after a single constant fix) on every input of a stated domain (up to $10^{16}$ inputs, or every graph or grid up to a size bound), in a minute of CPU or less each. The certificates also say where a network stops being exact: the shortest-path network is exact iff the distance is at most 4,096 and fails at the predicted hops. Thirty new specifications were each written by a fresh session of one model family (Claude Opus 5.5). Twenty-five first submissions are certified exact for any summation order; the five tax schedules stay within \$0.11 of the true tax at every whole dollar in one fixed float32 run. An open 27B model passes 23 of the 30, and 25 with more thinking and code execution, so the method transfers in part. We also prove two limits of learning from examples: input coordinates never active in training cannot be learned from more in-range data, and Luhn-type checksums have exponentially small target-dependent gradient variance across their family. Tuned gradient descent on the same architectures agrees with both, which cover two of our five failure classes.
  </details>

- **[When the Proxy Is Wrong: Mismatch-Corrected Bandits for Adaptive Data Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34707)**  `arXiv:2611.34707`  
  _Amine Saadi, Elissa Mhanna, Raphaël Féraud, Gwénolé Lecorvé_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Data allocation methods often use a small proxy model to select training data for a larger target model. However, this proxy can rank data differently from the target, leading to suboptimal training performance. To address this problem, we model the mismatch between the proxy and target models and incorporate it into the allocation decision. To do so, the problem is cast as a multi-fidelity bandit, where each arm is a data intervention. The proxy reward is observed every round, whereas the target reward is revealed only on rare audits of the same update. These paired observations identify arm-wise mismatches without assuming a shared offset or preservation of rankings. Mismatch-corrected bandits correct the proxy with paired residuals, audit only uncertain decisions, and pace the audit budget over training. From a theoretical viewpoint, we prove a regret decomposition and lower bounds under stationarity. These bounds show that proxy-only allocation can incur linear regret and that a minimum number of paired audits is necessary. Under abrupt changes, using the audit budget early can also incur linear regret. A sliding-window policy that spreads audits over training achieves regret of order $\sqrt{\Gamma_T T\log T}$ where $\Gamma_T$ denotes the number of change points. Experimentally, we test the approach in a closed-loop proof of concept on CivilComments-WILDS, where BERT-Small guides the training of BERT-Large. Mismatch correction improves worst-group accuracy over a target-only policy with the same target-model budget. Spreading audits over training improves worst-group accuracy by 6.3 to 10.5 percentage points at the same audit count.
  </details>

- **[Maco-RL: Scaling Agent Capabilities with Mixed-Task Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34703)**  `arXiv:2611.34703`  
  _Jiacheng Zhang, Qixing Zhou, Haiyang Wang, Qipeng Gu, Shuzhe Wu, Feiyang Pan, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Mixed-task reinforcement learning (MixRL) directly trains a unified policy across domains to continually expand agent capabilities without training separate specialists or requiring an extra distillation stage. Despite its appeal, scaling MixRL poses significant challenges in achieving stable and efficient mixed-task learning, effectively allocating rollout compute, and supporting continual domain expansion. To address these challenges, we propose Maco-RL, an approach that effectively scales MixRL. Specifically, Maco-RL employs a quota-based scheduler for asynchronous rollouts across multiple task domains, thereby stabilizing training by balancing gradient contributions and mitigating off-policy effects. Along an orthogonal axis, Maco-RL further introduces Tri-Buffer Sampling (TBS) to allocate compute among samples with varying levels of mastery, promoting sustained frontier exploration while preserving acquired capabilities. Experiments on five benchmarks show Maco-RL raises Qwen3.5-27B's overall score from 43.6 to 54.2 and then to 60.1 with continual expansion, reaching the frontier held by Qwen3.8-27B, which is further pushed outward by +5.7. Maco-RL also outperforms single-task RL with less compute for policy updates. These results support MixRL as a practical and compute-efficient post-training approach with substantial potential to strengthen general agent capabilities.
  </details>

- **[Effect of class proportion shifts on classifier curvature](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34702)**  `arXiv:2611.34702`  
  _Maxim Bolshim, Alexander Kugaevskikh_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Changing the class mix can alter mean loss without changing the classifier. To distinguish this reweighting from changes in the model itself, we studied ten-class CIFAR-10 classification in separate branches for two target classes, measuring the trace of the loss Hessian with respect to the output-layer parameters on fixed images of each target class. Across ten new initialisations, after 60 updates to the output layer with frozen features, the trace changed by -0.152% on average in branches where the target class share rose from 10% to 19%, and by +0.071% in branches where it fell to 1%, relative to each branch's initial trace. These changes do not isolate the effect of class share from that of the assigned training images. We developed a forecast based on initial class gradients after examining the first experiment's results and then tested it prospectively without modification. For direct increases from 10% to 19%, rather than increases after a deficit, its mean absolute error was 0.022 percentage points on the initial-trace scale, compared with 0.152 for a zero-change forecast and 0.104 for equally weighted gradients. Using the assigned class proportions improved the forecast of how much the trace would change.
  </details>

- **[Evacuation Traffic Prediction for Dynamic Transportation Networks over Multiple Hurricanes: A Generalized Graph Learning Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34687)**  `arXiv:2611.34687`  
  _Md Nafees Fuad Rafi, Samiul Hasan_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  High traffic demand during hurricane evacuations causes severe congestion on major highways, leading to delays and safety risks for evacuees. Predicting evacuation traffic in real-time can significantly enhance evacuation management efforts. However, evacuation traffic is highly dynamic and uncertain due to evolving hurricane characteristics and diverse population response. Each hurricane has unique characteristics and evacuation contexts, resulting in different spatial-temporal traffic patterns. Moreover, the structure of detector-based transportation networks varies across multiple hurricanes. Hence, a model trained on the data from one hurricane may not generalize well for others. This study proposes a generalized dynamic graph learning framework using traffic detectors and evacuation data from 12 historical hurricanes. Leveraging the dynamic nature of transportation network, we develop a Graph Convolutional Long Short-Term Memory (GCN-LSTM) model that predicts evacuation traffic up to 6 hours in advance. For an unseen hurricane (Milton, 2024), the model shows strong generalizability, achieving an RMSE of 280.6 and R2 of 0.96 for 1-hour prediction, and an RMSE of 459.8 and R2 of 0.89 for overall 6-hours prediction. We also introduce a modular training approach, where we evaluate performance improvements by sequentially incorporating data from multiple hurricanes. The proposed model outperforms state-of-the-art baseline models for overall 6-hour prediction horizons. Ablation experiments show an 8.4% improvement in RMSE for the proposed dynamic GCN-LSTM model compared to its static counterpart. Traffic management officials can use the developed model to understand future traffic conditions during hurricane evacuation in advance and take proactive measures to reduce delays during evacuation.
  </details>

- **[Provably Efficient Concave Utility Reinforcement Learning with Linear Function Approximation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34678)**  `arXiv:2611.34678`  
  _Max Qiushi Lin, Ahmed Magd, Sharan Vaswani_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Concave utility reinforcement learning (CURL) unifies a diverse range of problems, including standard reinforcement learning (RL), imitation learning, and maximum entropy exploration. Unlike standard RL, CURL generally requires estimating high-dimensional state-action occupancy measures. Consequently, existing methods for CURL either sidestep the exploration problem, are restricted to the tabular setting, or lack computationally efficient policy optimization. To address this, we study CURL in finite-horizon episodic bilinear MDPs, where the transition model admits a low-dimensional representation in known feature spaces. We use the bilinear structure to efficiently estimate occupancy measures via low-dimensional feature expectations, and propose a model-based optimistic concave utility policy optimization (OCUPO) framework. We first instantiate OCUPO in the on-policy setting, where each iteration uses independent trajectories to estimate the concave utility policy gradient, and prove an $\widetilde{O}(\epsilon^{-4})$ sample complexity. To improve sample efficiency, we then instantiate OCUPO in the off-policy setting. We propose a novel backward feature regression subroutine that reuses trajectories collected by past policies to estimate the occupancy measure of the current policy. Under suitable technical assumptions on the policy class (satisfied, e.g., by log-linear policies with sufficiently expressive features), we prove that the resulting algorithm achieves an $\widetilde{O}(\epsilon^{-2})$ sample complexity, up to a controllable projection error. We further extend our framework to linear MDPs and show that the resulting off-policy algorithm retains the same sample complexity. In these settings, the dependence on $\epsilon$ matches that for standard RL with linear function approximation. Moreover, our algorithms do not rely on the integral oracle required by prior work.
  </details>

- **[Learning to Be Truncated: Preparing LLM Checkpoints for SVD Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34667)**  `arXiv:2611.34667`  
  _Chenyue Fang, Danila Mishin, Babak Falsafi_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Compression based on singular value decomposition (SVD) often requires subsequent fine-tuning or weight correction to mitigate performance degradation. Budget-specific optimization must be repeated for different compression ratios. We introduce LLift, which prepares a pretrained model for SVD compression across ratios without further fine-tuning. LLift fine-tunes a low-rank approximation at a single ratio using the original model as a teacher. We merge the learned updates into the original weights while preserving the complementary components excluded from the training forward pass. We apply SVD to the prepared model's target matrices and reuse the decompositions at different truncation ranks. On LLaMA-7B, we demonstrate accuracy gains across three compression ratios using a single prepared model. The gains extend across model families, model sizes, and SVD compression operators. We analyze gradients and an early training update to provide local evidence that updates learned at one ratio can benefit compression at other ratios. These results show that LLift can improve compression across deployment budgets without fine-tuning each compressed model separately.
  </details>

- **[Do We Still Need Reinforcement Learning When We Can Read the World Model?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34656)**  `arXiv:2611.34656`  
  _Mingchao Zhang, Miduo Cui, Kangze He, Yuanjun Li, Dapeng Li, Ce Zhang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Reinforcement learning has achieved remarkable success in sequential decision-making, but learning effective policies often requires substantial interaction experience. Model-based reinforcement learning alleviates this dependence by leveraging world models, which are typically used to support planning or policy optimization. In this paper, we investigate an alternative paradigm in which autonomous LLM-based coding agents directly synthesize control policies by reasoning over readable world models. By examining environment source code, these agents translate environmental knowledge into executable decision rules and iteratively refine their policies using online feedback or offline data, without task-specific RL training. Experiments across diverse decision-making benchmarks show that synthesized policies match or outperform conventional RL methods while requiring substantially less experience. Further analyses reveal interpretable decision rules and how they evolve through feedback-driven refinement. Comparisons with policies generated without source code access and experiments under challenging conditions further demonstrate the benefits of readable world models. These findings suggest that direct policy synthesis can reduce reliance on trial and error, challenging the necessity of task-specific RL training.
  </details>

- **[Distractor-Robust Reinforcement Learning via Variational Bisimulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34641)**  `arXiv:2611.34641`  
  _Benjamin Freed, Vivaan Singh, Dean Zadok, Roberto Calandra, Jeff Schneider, Howie Choset_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) promises data efficiency and generalization, but typical reconstruction-based objectives encourage models to waste representational capacity on task-irrelevant distractors. We introduce VIBES (Variational Inference for Bisimulation-based Encoded States), a new objective that replaces pixel reconstruction with an adversarial term, which enforces that latent states suffice to predict both rewards and the next latent state. We show that this objective measures how far the encoder is from reward and dynamics sufficiency, and that whenever exact sufficiency is attainable, its global optima induce bisimulation relations on histories. Combined with a fixed-capacity latent bottleneck, this encourages latent states to retain task-relevant information while discarding irrelevant variation. Our method serves as a drop-in replacement for Dreamer's model-learning component, achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Distracting Control Suite, and extends to visually complex manipulation in Realistic ManiSkill. Unlike prior approaches, it does not rely on image-specific augmentations and applies equally well to high-dimensional vector-state tasks, demonstrated on a 100-link swimmer robot. Finally, latent-space analyses (UMAP embeddings and nearest-neighbor probes) confirm that the learned representations are sensitive to task-relevant structure while invariant to distractors.
  </details>

- **[Predicting acute food crises and discovering actionable drivers with causal machine learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34629)**  `arXiv:2611.34629`  
  _Mélissande Machefer, Michele Ronco, Michele Meroni, Jordi Cerdà-Bautista, Francesco Collivignarelli, Chungmann Kim, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Acute food insecurity is driven by a compound of conflict, adverse climate events, displacement, and economic shocks. We enrich the open-access Harmonized Food Insecurity Dataset with driver variables (monthly, subnational, 80 countries, 2007--2024) and develop missing-data-resilient machine learning pipelines forecasting crisis occurrence at 3, 6, and 9-month lead times using both FEWS NET and, for the first time at scale, IPC/CH classifications. Pipelines, evaluated through nested cross-validation, outperform no-skill baselines by 15 to 50 percentage points in PR-AUC, with performance correlated with crisis prevalence rather than the classification system. TreeSHAP-based explainability reveals compound, geography-specific predictive signal profiles, with three recurrent forecasting archetypes. Comparing predictive importance against doubly robust causal estimates of actionable drivers, we find that acute conflict events, having the weakest predictive signals, emerge as primary causal drivers of crisis classification whilst agroclimatology is the sole dimension in which predictive importance and causal effect align.
  </details>

- **[Automated Batch-Variable Selection for ComBat-Based Radiomic Harmonization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34618)**  `arXiv:2611.34618`  
  _Jose Lozano-Montoya, Gemma Urbanos, Carmen Prieto-de-la-Lastra, Emilio Soria-Olivas, Ana Jimenez-Pastor_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  ComBat harmonizes multicentre radiomic features, but batch variables are usually chosen manually, without a standardized criterion across image acquisition parameters. We propose ParsiComBat, which selects acquisition parameters for ComBat, balancing batch-effect removal against feature-structure preservation and abstaining when technical variation is negligible.ParsiComBat ranks candidate acquisition parameters by batch effect, filters redundancy, and scores sequential ComBat corrections. We evaluated it in three experiments: in simulations, testing whether it recovered a known batch variable and abstained without one; in CT (NSCLC-Radiomics) and MRI (MAMA-MIA) cohorts, comparing batch-effect removal against manufacturer (manual), every feasible parameter (greedy) and AutoCombat; and in clinical prediction, internally and externally.In simulations, ParsiComBat identified the true batch variable in 92.9% of positive trials and abstained in 99.2% of null controls. In CT, correcting for reconstruction kernel reduced mean k-nearest neighbour batch-effect test from 0.276 to 0.032, almost matching greedy correction of six variables. In MRI, correcting for slice thickness and manufacturer reduced it from 0.680 to 0.325, slightly more than manual selection but less than greedy correction of seven variables. Removing technical variation did not improve clinical discrimination: no strategy, including raw features, differed significantly from ParsiComBat in area under the curve.ParsiComBat provides a data-driven framework that removes technical batch effects using minimal acquisition parameters, preserving feature structure and clinical discrimination. It selects variables verifiable against the acquisition protocol and abstains when no correction is needed, supporting transparent, reproducible multicentre radiomics.
  </details>

- **[Learning from Crowds with Unsupervised Item Response Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34602)**  `arXiv:2611.34602`  
  _Pascal Wullschleger, Majid Zarharan, Donnacha Daly, Marc Pouly, Jennifer Foster_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Item Response Theory (IRT) is the study of tests, including the properties of both test items and test takers. Crowdsourced labelling can be cast as an unsupervised IRT problem: annotators play the role of test takers with varying ability, and annotation tasks play the role of items with varying difficulty. We evaluate unsupervised variants of standard logistic IRT models for latent trait recovery and label inference on six datasets with crowdsourced labels and known ground truths. Unsupervised IRT models can recover annotator and item traits (e.g., ability, difficulty and discrimination) reliably across most datasets when compared to supervised variants trained on the ground truth. IRT models seem to be more stable in label inference compared to most baselines, but might not be the best possible choice depending on the dataset. We further propose to use IRT models to inform classifiers during training and compare against existing crowd-learning methods. We find that crowd-learning methods can improve F1 over majority-vote baselines, but no method significantly improves both F1 and calibration. IRT-informed curriculum methods seem to preserve calibration better than other crowd-learning methods, but are not at the frontier regarding F1, and the best crowd-learning methods in terms of F1 seem to be miscalibrated.
  </details>

- **[ChemoMAE: Self-Supervised Spectral Representation Learning Reveals Chemical Heterogeneity in Historical Wood](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34581)**  `arXiv:2611.34581`  
  _Ryuji Yamaguchi, Miyuki Matsuo_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  In historical timber buildings, multiple environmental factors act over centuries on wood whose chemical composition varies across anatomical regions, producing complex patterns of degradation. Understanding how timber members degrade is important for the effective conservation and restoration of historical buildings, yet the mechanisms underlying these patterns remain unclear. To investigate these mechanisms, we used self-supervised learning to establish a common basis for comparing specimens from timber members that differ in wood species and service history. We examined transverse sections of 49 wood specimens from several historical buildings in Japan using near-infrared hyperspectral imaging. ChemoMAE, a self-supervised Transformer, learns pixelwise spectral representations through masked denoising that exploits multicollinearity among spectral variables. Clustering these representations yields spatial maps without predefined chemical-state categories. Because anatomy and degradation can produce spatially continuous regions, we formulated Local Label Agreement (LLA) to quantify agreement among labels assigned to neighboring pixels. Using spectra alone, ChemoMAE yielded higher mean LLA than baseline methods on validation specimens. We then trained ChemoMAE anew and fitted cluster centers across all specimens. Spatial structures consistent with wood anatomy and the expected effects of surface exposure emerged in the resulting maps. By cross-referencing regional spectra and spatial distributions across specimens in light of wood anatomy, service histories, and prior studies, we proposed models of internal and surface degradation as mechanistic hypotheses. This exploratory AI for Science framework gives researchers a basis for linking latent patterns learned through self-supervision with domain knowledge when investigating how material states form.
  </details>

- **[Tune for Retention, Not Just Gain: SFT Forgets Far Less than You Think](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34579)**  `arXiv:2611.34579`  
  _Nirmit Joshi, Nathan Srebro, Eran Malach_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Catastrophic forgetting, the drastic loss of previously acquired capabilities when learning new ones, is a central challenge in language model fine-tuning. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is widely believed to be prone to such forgetting. Recent works have attributed this to the off-policy nature of SFT, arguing that on-policy learning is key to continual learning. In this paper, we challenge this premise. We show that while maximizing new-task performance can induce catastrophic forgetting, alternative hyperparameter choices (lower learning rate and batch size) can yield similar gains with little to no forgetting. With hyperparameters selected jointly for gain and retention, vanilla SFT retains prior capabilities far better than previously suggested and can be competitive with Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (SDFT), an on-policy approach designed to mitigate forgetting. While SDFT can be more robust to hyperparameter choices, it also requires a retention-aware criterion to identify hyperparameter configurations that avoid catastrophic forgetting. Our results challenge the view that on-policy training is what enables learning with retention and raise broader questions about what drives catastrophic forgetting during fine-tuning.
  </details>

- **[Investigating the efficacy of vortex beam speckle patterns for the recognition of atmospheric turbulence and fractional topological charge with a deep learning model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34573)**  `arXiv:2611.34573`  
  _Ratikanta Swain, Allarakha Shikder, Naseem Babu, Niladri Sarkar, Aryan Raj, Raghavan K. Easwaran_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Fractional topological charge (TC) enlarges the usable mode set of orbital angular momentum (OAM) links, but reading it reliably after atmospheric turbulence remains difficult. Interferometric and diffractive methods need an undistorted beam and a careful alignment, while most learned approaches treat integer or coarsely spaced charges and do not include turbulence. Here we ask whether the charge of a scalar vortex beam can be regressed directly from a single speckle image, and at which turbulence strength this stops working. We propagate vortex beams over 1500~m through 150 von Kármán phase screens, scatter them with a fixed random diffuser, and record $256\times256$, 16-bit speckle images for TC from 0 to 10 in steps of 0.01 and turbulence strengths $D/r_0$ from 0 to 50; the results reported here use a subset of 20\,000 images, and a data set of $10^{6}$ images is in preparation. A convolutional neural network estimates the TC and, through an auxiliary head, the turbulence category. On charges withheld from training, the mean absolute error is 0.031 without turbulence (with a common intensity scale) and rises to 0.78 at $D/r_0=10$ and 1.85 at $D/r_0=50$, against 2.5 for a constant prediction, and the turbulence category is identified correctly in 78\% of the images. The results show that, at the present training size, the charge is read accurately only without turbulence, and that the charge and the turbulence oth act on the speckle grain size, which may limit the readout. Experimental validation and the extension to vector vortex beams are left for future work.
  </details>

- **[Resilience Analysis Through Automated Stage Identification and Quantitative Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34527)**  `arXiv:2611.34527`  
  _Anna Strzoda, Krzysztof Grochla, Rafael Munoz-Carpena_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  This paper introduced an ML-based approach, designed to be domain- and threat-agnostic, for automated recognition of PARA (Plan/Prepare, Absorb, Recover, Adapt) resilience stages in system-performance time series, enabling subsequent quantitative resilience analysis across different systems. We investigate four ML models for resilience stage recognition: Random Forest (RF), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost). We then use the ML models' predictions to quantify system resilience by computing corresponding resilience metrics from system-performance data observed before, during, and after disruptive events. We evaluate the proposed approach using datasets from two distinct operational domain network systems and an airport transportation system, demonstrating its domain-agnostic applicability to resilience assessment. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of resilience stage classification, with the best F1-scores ranging from 74.3% to 99.4% across all resilience stages. The overall resilience metrics R_t and RL are estimated, with the best models' MAPE ranging from 0.35-0.82% on IEEE 802.11 and LTE to 1.65-9.56% for the airport. These results provide a basis for threat-agnostic resilience analysis of complex engineering systems, enabling further assessment of how effectively a system withstands, absorbs, and recovers from disruptive events and stress conditions.
  </details>

- **[SMOTE 25 Years of Magic: What Has Been Done, What the Evidence Shows, and Whom It Reached](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34511)**  `arXiv:2611.34511`  
  _Thanapong Intharah, Pharamut Makjaroen, Kanvara Thawarorit, Supawit Chaingam_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Background. SMOTE was published in this journal in 2002 and reviewed here at its fifteenth anniversary in 2018. At twenty-five it is cited by more than 34,000 indexed works, half of them outside computer science. Objectives. To establish what the methods built on SMOTE change, how strong the evidence for them is, and whom the technique has reached. Methods. We audited a curated corpus of 76 papers, 37 of which propose a SMOTE-family generator, and tested its coverage with a systematic search of 22,426 records in the PRISMA 2020 format. From the corpus we collected 1,756 dataset entries, 1,511 published comparisons with SMOTE and the evaluation design of 71 studies; from the search we drew 300 applications of SMOTE at random. We used an agentic AI approach to extract, screen and code under our written rules, and we report how each step was checked. Results. Every variant re-decides some of the six decisions of the SMOTE rule, and 24 of the 37 are only ever run on two classes. In their own papers, proposed methods beat SMOTE in 79.0% of the decided comparisons, but independent studies find that the gains shrink with strong learners and tuned thresholds, and that resampling damages calibration. The corpus holds 52 of the 3,097 records that pass the screen and covers the early years closely, the recent ones thinly. The reach is very wide, but a benefit at the level of outcomes is undemonstrated, four harms are documented, and an estimated 37% of applications resample the whole data set before splitting it. Conclusions. For tabular classification, a new SMOTE variant should no longer count as a contribution in itself: a new generator should be tested one decision at a time against class weighting and a tuned threshold with a strong learner, with calibration reported. We close with a selection guide, a reporting checklist of fifteen items and a research agenda.
  </details>

- **[Auditing Identity and Timing Signals in Operational Logs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34493)**  `arXiv:2611.34493`  
  _Andrew Hendel_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Models that predict events from operational logs, such as sepsis in ICU records or failures in hard drives, can score well by recognizing which patient or drive a record came from, or when it was recorded, instead of predicting the event. I introduce two simple audits that measure how much of this information a dataset carries before any event-prediction model is trained, and apply them to seven public datasets in six domains. One asks whether a classifier can tell that two records came from the same unit; the other asks which of two records from the same unit came later. Under the stated nulls, both have expected AUC 0.5. In ICU data, the identity audit flags a common preprocessing step: carrying the last measurement forward raises identity AUC from 0.916 to 0.993. On a 12-hour sepsis forecasting task, carrying forward makes a model look 0.163 AUC better than raw values when a patient's hours are split between training and test, but only 0.046 better when patients are held out. The exaggeration under patient overlap also appears in a second ICU dataset with mortality as the outcome. On the sepsis task, a chronological control with complete follow-up, in which training sees only a patient's earlier, resolved hours, shows no positive mean overlap gap. Timing is a strong predictor: with complete follow-up, hour of stay and measurement counts alone, with no clinical value, score 0.761 on held-out patients, and adding the raw clinical values changes that by +0.018. Outside the ICU, 95% of drives and 75% of loans have records on both sides of a calendar cut, and the overlap gap persists under a calendar split. The audits show which features and preprocessing choices to check; the evaluation protocol decides the consequences. I release the code, a library that runs the audits on any table with a unit column and a time column, and a guide to using the audits.
  </details>

- **[Strong Starts, Simple Recipes: Unified Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation from Multimodal Specialists](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34397)**  `arXiv:2611.34397`  
  _Wenzheng Chang, Taiqiang Wu, Yuqi Xu, Yongfu Zhu, Zelin Peng, Ji Zhao, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) integrates separately trained domain specialists into a single unified model. Existing methods focus on refining the distillation procedure while initializing the student from a base model or a multi-domain SFT checkpoint, which leaves capability integration largely to distillation itself. Instead, we treat the starting point as a design variable and propose Unified MOPD (Uni-MOPD), which pairs a strong start with a simple recipe: a training-free uniform merge of specialists from the same base model initializes the student, and short MOPD with uniform domain sampling and full-vocabulary reverse KL refines it. Across five multimodal domains and 19 benchmarks, our study establishes three findings. (1) The starting point matters more than subsequent training choices: before any training, the uniform merge already matches the score that the base model reaches after 200 MOPD updates, and after short distillation it matches higher-scoring, search-based starts. (2) Short MOPD recovers most of the capabilities the merge leaves unintegrated; it improves every domain, with the largest gains where the domain teacher still leads. (3) From a strong start, uniform domain sampling and full-vocabulary reverse KL match or exceed every evaluated sampling strategy and divergence, without schedules, per-token weighting, or truncation hyperparameters. Uni-MOPD outperforms Open-MOPD at the same training budget while training 3.3 times faster than its released code. We will release the training framework, specialist checkpoints, and unified student.
  </details>

- **[RAWPrism: A Three-Task Dataset and a Unified Model for RAW-Domain Image Fusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34359)**  `arXiv:2611.34359`  
  _Tianyi Hu, Yangdong Li, Shuyan Liu, Zihan Cao, Jingze Liang, Shaojie Wu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Research on multi-exposure fusion (MEF), multi-focus fusion (MFF), and infrared-visible image fusion (IVIF) has largely focused on rendered RGB images, while unified fusion across these tasks in the RAW domain before image signal processing (ISP) remains relatively underexplored. To support research in this setting, we introduce the RAWPrism dataset, covering all three tasks, and the RAWPrism model, a lightweight unified multi-task fusion network. The RAWPrism dataset comprises 422 usable MEF scenes and 150 registered MFF pairs from our RAW captures, together with 1,500 FMB-derived IVIF samples, in which the visible RAW inputs are reconstructed by ReRAW and their RGB counterparts rendered by CycleISP. Scene-level partitions and task-specific rendering and scoring protocols connect these resources to method development and evaluation. To our knowledge, the RAWPrism model is the first to unify MEF, MFF, and IVIF directly in the RAW domain. It combines a CFA-aware representation, task-conditioned source gating, and a shared backbone to support all three tasks with one 3.58M-parameter checkpoint. Together, the dataset and model support the study of shared fusion mechanisms across exposure, focus, and spectral complementarity.
  </details>

- **[Inverse Reinforcement Learning with State-Dependent Foresight for Human Decision-Making](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34351)**  `arXiv:2611.34351`  
  _Jinil Kim, Jinwoo Jeong, Hyeongjun Yun, Min-hwan Oh, Woo-Young Ahn_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Computational modeling of behavior represents individuals with a model fitted to their observed behavior and characterizes them through its parameters. Naturalistic tasks incorporate the complexity of real environments and yield high-dimensional behavioral trajectories. Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) infers the latent reward function underlying these trajectories. Standard IRL, however, assumes effectively infinite-horizon planning, whereas human foresight is both bounded and state-dependent. Here we introduce SC-AIRL (State-Conditional Adversarial IRL), which builds these two cognitive properties into the planner. Per-depth policies share one reward but differ in how far ahead they sum it explicitly. A state-conditional router mixes them according to the current state. Across held-out episodes in pedestrian crossing and highway overtaking tasks, SC-AIRL improves imitation over Standard AIRL, raising top-1 accuracy from 0.549 to 0.647 and from 0.629 to 0.718, respectively, while more closely reproducing participant behavior in rollouts. Inferred planning depth correlates with self-reported anxiety and motor impulsivity. SC-AIRL thus reproduces human behavior more closely than Standard AIRL while providing an interpretable, model-derived measure of state-dependent foresight.
  </details>

- **[RAP: Radial-Angular Random Projection for Hyperbolic Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34298)**  `arXiv:2611.34298`  
  _Jiahong Liu, Wenhao Yu, Yifan Li, Yanyu Chen, Rex Ying, Menglin Yang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Random projection is a basic compression primitive for Euclidean representation learning, with the Johnson--Lindenstrauss lemma giving a target dimension $k=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log n)$ independent of the ambient dimension. As hyperbolic representations gain increasing attention in modern Transformers, vision-language models, and large language models, the same need for oblivious dimensionality reduction arises, but no analogous primitive yet exists for hyperbolic representations. We study this gap. Two natural attempts fail in dual ways: a tangent-space scheme gives a clean local guarantee but is chart-bound and pays a curvature penalty, while a fully hyperbolic projection in the hyperboloid model is geometrically native but mixes radial and angular error before feeding them into the conditioning of $\operatorname{arcosh}$. We propose radial-angular random projection (RAP), which preserves the radial coordinate exactly and applies a Euclidean random projection only to the angular direction, lifting the result back to the target hyperboloid. RAP is hyperbolic-to-hyperbolic by construction, costs one Gaussian matrix-vector product, and reduces hyperbolic compression to a normalized angular JL question on $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$. We prove a finite-set RAP guarantee with explicit $\sinh(\sqrt{c}\,r_x)\sinh(\sqrt{c}\,r_y)$ conditioning, complemented by a local tangent-space JL theorem and an arcosh-conditioning lemma for the fully hyperbolic comparator. Across an origin-centered broad-radius point cloud, a balanced tree, a clustered Gaussian, and the WordNet noun hierarchy, RAP attains the lowest mean relative distortion in every $(n,k)$ cell, reducing distortion over the strongest hyperbolic baseline by approximately $48\%$--$49\%$ on broad-radius data. RAP also scales to million-point datasets and improves retrieval on vision--language representations over hyperbolic projection baselines.
  </details>

- **[Scaling Looped MoE Language Models under Matched Budgets: Information Flow and Parameter Allocation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34276)**  `arXiv:2611.34276`  
  _Shipeng Bai, Jiayu Qin, Hong Liu, Xili Wang, Jianchao Tan, Jiacheng Li, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Looped Transformers decouple computational depth from parameter count, and prior studies have demonstrated promising performance gains with increased computation. However, systematic design principles for configuring these models under strict iso-parameter and iso-FLOP constraints remain scarce. We contribute to this direction by improving information flow in looped models and systematically studying loop parameter configurations. Specifically, we refine this information flow via gated inner-loop state updates and a cross-stage residual connection. Building on this design, controlled studies identify a configuration combining a single-pass Core depth of 25%-35% of the total unrolled depth with reallocating saved parameters into extra routed experts per layer, improving performance at zero extra compute while preserving compatibility with existing training infrastructure. Evaluated after 1T pre-training tokens, our 69B MLA and 51B KDA Mixture-of-Experts models outperform budget-matched non-recurrent baselines by an average of 1.16 and 2.29 percentage points across four benchmarks, respectively. Further reproduction experiments on a common backbone with a 200B-token training budget show that our method achieves lower perplexity than other looped methods. Code for these reproduction experiments is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[LatentCP-DPO: Conformal Pessimism for DPO with Finite-Sample Guarantees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34275)**  `arXiv:2611.34275`  
  _Hongwei Xu, Jingyi Liu, Vincent Y. F. Tan, Zai Yang, Yulian Wu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) learns a response policy from human preference data, but with a limited dataset it can overfit to noisy or weakly informative preference labels. We introduce LatentCP-DPO, a framework that combines conformal prediction with pessimistic preference optimization for Bradley-Terry (BT) pairwise feedback and Plackett-Luce (PL) ranking feedback. Building on LatentCP's construction of uncertainty sets for unobserved model parameters, we address how to incorporate this uncertainty into preference optimization and characterize its effect on policy performance. Under exchangeability and a correctly specified preference model, we construct uncertainty sets for latent relative rewards with finite-sample marginal coverage from conformal prediction sets for observable preferences. We then learn a response policy by maximizing the worst-case expected preference log-likelihood over these uncertainty sets, using an independent collection of prompts and candidate responses without preference labels. Under suitable assumptions, we establish finite-sample upper bounds on regularized policy suboptimality that separate policy-class approximation error, conformal uncertainty, and statistical estimation error. For BT feedback, we further establish a worst-case lower bound for LatentCP-DPO that matches the upper bound's reciprocal dependence on the number of unlabeled optimization examples. The lower bound also shows that the uncertainty sets can induce a bias that persists as the optimization sample grows. Together, these results characterize both the statistical accuracy and potential limitations of preference optimization using conformal uncertainty sets. Experiments support the benefits of the proposed framework in finite preference datasets.
  </details>

- **[LLM-coupled interpretable tool wear monitoring with multi-evidence reasoning in CNC machining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34270)**  `arXiv:2611.34270`  
  _Yuntong Chen, Yingqi Li, Qiwen Shen, Guobin Zhao, Xitian Tian, Lijiang Huang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Interpretable tool wear assessment in CNC machining is challenging. Existing diagnostic models have high accuracy but provide limited guidance for tool replacement. This study proposes a two layer framework combining deep learning wear classification and LLM assisted reasoning. The first layer uses PCA Loading feature selection and optimized GRU to recognize three wear states, achieving 98.38 percent macro F1 score on the PHM2010 dataset. The second layer uses LLMs to generate natural language reports and replacement suggestions from classification results and feature trends. Engineer evaluation shows the reports outperform rule templates. Cross dataset tests on NASA milling data support the generalizability of this framework.
  </details>

- **[Text-Conditioned Low-Rank Adaptation of Time-Series Foundation Models for Multimodal Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34206)**  `arXiv:2611.34206`  
  _Kunqi Li, Bin Liang, Zhidong Li_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Time-series foundation models (TSFMs) provide transferable numerical forecasting priors. However, forecast-relevant information may be conveyed in text without being reflected in the observed series. Many multimodal forecasting methods integrate such context through model inputs or intermediate representations. We investigate a complementary mechanism: text-conditioned parameter adaptation. We propose Context-to-LoRA for Time Series (C2LoRA-TS), which encodes text and generates temporary Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) updates for selected weight matrices of a frozen TSFM. Both the numerical backbone and text encoder remain frozen, and the method exactly recovers the frozen TSFM output when context is absent. Evaluated on Time-MMD across nine domains and three TSFM architectures, C2LoRA-TS achieves lower aggregate forecasting error than the frozen-TSFM and Static LoRA baselines for every architecture and seed. Replacing the instance-specific text with a single globally fixed context degrades performance for every architecture. These results support text-conditioned parameter generation as a viable strategy for multimodal forecasting with frozen TSFMs.
  </details>

- **[Agent-as-a-Verifier: From Scores to Evidence for General Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34132)**  `arXiv:2611.34132`  
  _Yuxuan Sun, Chen, Nagarajan Natarajan, Sushrut Karmalkar, Niranjani Prasad, Amit Sharma, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Verification is increasingly critical across various inference and learning paradigms, such as test-time scaling, recursive intelligence and automated research, where feedback can improve efficiency and optimization. Common score-based verifiers, or discriminative reward models, predict a scalar reward for an output. While useful for filtering, rewarding, and ranking, such scores provide no explicit, auditable evidentiary basis for the judgment. In parallel, although existing generative process reward models offer text feedback, most designs do not fully exploit agentic capabilities, such as tool use and iterative reasoning, which are essential for fact-checking and fine-grained claim verification. In this paper, we address these limitations by introducing Agent-as-a-Verifier, an agentic, certificate-producing verification system that places role-separated LLM agents inside a formal-methods-inspired claim-obligation-certificate protocol. Given a generation candidate, Agent-as-a-Verifier produces a certificate by extracting a verdict-blind dependency graph of claims, independently compiling the task's acceptance contract, and deriving checkable obligations. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, Agent-as-a-Verifier achieves higher accuracy than the state-of-the-art approach. Across different downstream applications, the augmented agent also outperforms the plain agent on FrontierMath and CyberGym. More importantly, Agent-as-a-Verifier is able to identify reward-hacking solutions that deceive the benchmark evaluator, highlighting its broader potential for iterative and recursive agent optimization. Code is available atthis https URL
  </details>

- **[MUSE: Multi-Task Uncertainty-Aware Self-Supervised Encoder for mmWave ISAC](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34122)**  `arXiv:2611.34122`  
  _Nabeel Nisar Bhat, Jalees Nehvi, Rafael Berkvens, Jeroen Famaey_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) allows a wireless system to use the same waveform for communication and environment sensing. At mmWave frequency bands, ISAC enables diverse human sensing tasks, such as localization, gesture recognition, and pose estimation, with high precision. However, each task requires training a dedicated model, typically from scratch on a task-specific dataset, with no mechanism to flag unreliable predictions. This hurts the scalability, transferability, and reliability of mmWave ISAC models. In this work, we propose MUSE (Multi-task Uncertainty-aware Self-supervised Encoder), a unified framework for mmWave human sensing. MUSE leverages a self-supervised transformer model with per-dataset tokenization and is trained via masked autoencoding across five datasets. During fine-tuning, MUSE uses evidential classification heads that enable uncertainty quantification. MUSE replaces N separate encoders with a single shared transformer encoder, an N-times backbone parameter reduction, while achieving a 9.7 percentage points improvement in classification performance compared to the task-specific model, showing that learning jointly across tasks improves per-task generalization. Across four classification tasks, MUSE produces reliable uncertainty estimates that enable selective prediction, improving accuracy by abstaining on the least confident 20% of predictions. We further improve the reliability of the model's confidence estimates using temperature scaling and conformal prediction. Finally, MUSE's uncertainty signal remains reliable even under cross-user deployment, assigning higher uncertainty to wrong predictions than to correct ones 78% of the time, and recovering 9.2 percentage points of accuracy through selective prediction, with no additional retraining on the unseen user.
  </details>

- **[Unstable Action Boundaries in Lethal Drone Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34121)**  `arXiv:2611.34121`  
  _Jacques Dumora, André-Louis Rochet, Simon Roburin_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Tool-using large language model (LLM) agents raise safety risks that are not captured by text-only refusal behavior, especially when tools can trigger high-impact actions. This concern is salient in military settings, where autonomous weapons raise the possibility of delegating force decisions to software agents. In this work, we study whether a drone agent's action boundary is stable under changes to the target descriptor. We evaluate recent and popular LLMs in a simulated perception-action pipeline over real-world drone imagery, where models can localize requested targets and invoke a simulated lethal tool. We find two concerning failure modes. First, some LLM agents invoke the lethal tool for ordinary generic descriptors such as \emph{people}, requiring no jailbreak at all. Second, an agent that initially appears conservative under protected descriptors can become unsafe under a simple semantic target shift.
  </details>

- **[SysBio-SR: Benchmarking Symbolic Regression for Trajectory Fidelity and Mechanism Recovery in Systems Biology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34106)**  `arXiv:2611.34106`  
  _Heng Rao, Dan Gao, Benjamin J Hoffman, Yu Gu, Zhenghao Liu, Ge Yu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Symbolic regression seeks to discover interpretable governing equations for dynamical systems from data. In systems biology, however, accurately reproducing system trajectories does not necessarily imply recovery of the underlying reaction mechanisms. Existing benchmarks evaluate numerical accuracy, expression complexity, or equation-level similarity, but not agreement between recovered reactions and reference mechanisms in biological systems. We introduce SysBio-SR, a benchmark of 198 literature-based biological ODE systems with reaction annotations spanning mass action, Michaelis--Menten, Hill, and complex kinetics. Trajectory fidelity is evaluated across all systems under in-distribution reconstruction and out-of-distribution (OOD) extrapolation, while mechanism recovery is assessed on the subset of 161 systems. We evaluate trajectory fidelity across 11 symbolic-discovery methods and assess mechanism recovery for three reaction-based methods. Joint analysis across systems highlights how severely trajectory-based evaluation overestimates true mechanism recovery. Motivated by these findings, we develop KineSelect, a framework that searches candidate reaction topologies under biologically grounded kinetic laws to select optimal mechanisms that balance trajectory fidelity with structural parsimony. Compared with the strongest baseline, KineSelect improves aggregate OOD extrapolation \(R^2\) by 19.2\% and overall reaction F1 score by 14.3\%.
  </details>

- **[Do Machine Learning Ensembles Beat Published Quotas? Target Parameterization, Censored Baselines, and Conformal Intervals Under Admissions Reform](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34104)**  `arXiv:2611.34104`  
  _Dat Tat Mai, James Jin Kang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Public admission capacity caps published prior to matriculation are widely used by ministries and institutional analysts as default intake projections in centralized postsecondary clearinghouses. Using an audited 2022 to 2026 Vietnamese undergraduate panel (26,895 program-year records across 309 universities) linked to strictly lagged t-1 occupational vacancy signals, this paper evaluates machine learning, multilevel, and censored econometric estimators against published quotas across 5,385 continuing 2024 programs (five-fold university-grouped cross-validation) and 3,348 matched (2,179 grain-consistent) 2025 programs strictly out of time. Because 62.8% of 2024 programs enroll their exact published quota, unanchored log-growth ensembles degrade accuracy, while the worst 5% generate half of total quota error via unfilled "phantom capacity." Controlled target ablations, including a single-factor test under widened non-binding clipping, show that parameterizing the log fill ratio ln(D_it / S_it) instead of log growth reduces 2024 MAE by 21.5% (14.86 to 11.67), aligns ML with Tobit, Cragg, REML HLM, and capped L1 baselines, and lifts combined tuition and institutional-tier TreeSHAP attribution from 2.5% to 45.8%. Hurdle stacking attains the lowest full-census 2024 MAE (H-Hard 11.29; H-Soft 11.32 vs. 12.35, p = 0.022, clearing 10% not 5% FDR; fold-overlap p = 0.134), whereas continuous QA-Stack outperforms H-Soft on mixed-reporting campuses, Tobit (median) ties H-Soft across both 90% MCS sets, and interior-only Cragg-ML lowers RMSE to 28.1. Under Vietnam's 2025 unified-clearing reform, exact filling falls to 10.4%, H-Soft and capped L1 tie quotas (p = 0.979), and 90% cluster-weighted conformal coverage drops from 89.3% to 74.6%. Across 257 reporting campuses, reconciled 2026 national totals (627,114 to 629,256) lie squarely within 604,533 to 662,044.
  </details>

- **[AlignPre: Skill-Aligned Post-Training for Latent-Free Generative Precipitation Nowcasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34101)**  `arXiv:2611.34101`  
  _Demin Yu, Kenghong Lin, Xutao Li_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Precipitation nowcasting requires accurate short-term predictions under rapidly evolving spatiotemporal dynamics. Generative diffusion models can produce detailed and competitive radar forecasts by modeling conditional distributions. However, most existing approaches rely on separately trained components, such as deterministic branches or latent compression modules. More fundamentally, distribution matching alone fails to explicitly optimize operational forecast skill. We propose AlignPre, a streamlined pixel-space nowcasting framework that bridges this gap via skill-aligned post-training (SAPT). AlignPre employs an end-to-end flow-matching forecaster with a hierarchical spatiotemporal architecture for distribution matching and direct radar-field synthesis, without latent compression. During post-training, SAPT exploits the analytic structure of forecast verification scores to construct a differentiable objective. By backpropagating gradients of this objective from radar fields to the generator, SAPT turns forecast verification into direct training feedback. Across three real-world benchmarks spanning different forecast horizons, AlignPre consistently surpasses state-of-the-art deterministic and generative baselines in forecast skill, demonstrating that aligning generative modeling with domain-specific verification provides an effective paradigm for meteorological forecasting.
  </details>

- **[Improving Tail-Augmented Speculative Drafting with Hidden State Mixing and Gradient Detach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34092)**  `arXiv:2611.34092`  
  _Yaniv Galron, Rabeeh Karimi Mahabadi, Maor Ashkenazi, Roger Waleffe, Talor Abramovich, Tiyasa Mitra, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Multi-token prediction (MTP) modules and EAGLE-style drafters support efficient speculative decoding by reusing target-model hidden states. Their autoregressive use, however, introduces a training-inference mismatch: training supplies sequences of hidden states from the backbone or a single MTP step, whereas inference attends to a target-model prefix followed by a growing tail of recurrently generated MTP states. EAGLE-3's training-time test (TTT) explicitly simulates this behavior during training, at the cost of additional memory and specialized attention masks. We introduce two training-only methods for improving autoregressive drafting. Hidden State Mixing (HSM) samples among backbone and MTP hidden states aligned to the same prediction target, exposing the drafter to mixtures of states from different MTP steps without explicitly simulating inference. Hidden State Gradient Detach (HSGD) is a regularization method that stochastically blocks gradients through hidden state and embedding pathways while preserving the forward computation. Neither method adds inference cost. In joint pretraining followed by supervised fine-tuning, HSGD yields the highest acceptance rates at early draft positions, while HSM performs best later in the draft. These acceptance rate trends favor HSM for long-draft-length serving and HSGD for short-draft-length serving. Furthermore, across four Nemotron models and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, HSM-based MTP boosting with a frozen backbone improves mean acceptance length by up to 52.2% over the co-trained MTP. For EAGLE-3 drafters, HSM offers competitive acceptance with TTT, with 48% lower peak reserved training memory in a four-step Qwen3-8B comparison. HSM implementations are publicly available in Megatron-LM and NVIDIA Model Optimizer.
  </details>

- **[CARE-WM: Same-Horizon Self-Conditioning with Constraint-Adaptive Regularization for Latent World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34054)**  `arXiv:2611.34054`  
  _Yuchen Lin, Kai Zhao_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Planning with latent world models requires both accurate multi-step predictions and latent distances that reflect physical proximity to the goal. However, models are typically trained on ground-truth observations but must rely on their own imaginations during planning, while closer latent distances do not necessarily correspond to better task outcomes. Existing methods resort to auxiliary training objectives or additional task-cost readouts, which respectively incur extra training overhead or leave the latent geometry itself misaligned with task cost. We introduce CARE-WM, a drop-in training method that meets both requirements without additional supervision, a separate cost model, or any change to LeWM's architecture and Euclidean-cost planner. CARE-WM trains the predictor on its own predictions and adaptively calibrates the strength of latent regularization. With a single hyperparameter configuration, CARE-WM improves mean planning success over LeWM across all evaluated continuous-control tasks and matches or exceeds the best results of other LeWM-family methods on most tasks. Further analyses show lower open-loop latent prediction error and closer agreement between latent-cost rankings and physical task costs.
  </details>

- **[Decentralized Clustered Federated Learning for Cellular Traffic Forecasting over LEO Constellations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34049)**  `arXiv:2611.34049`  
  _Jonas Kirch, Tiago Koketsu Rodrigues, Yuichi Kawamoto_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite constellations are positioned to act as orbital edge-compute nodes in emerging 6G non-terrestrial networks, supporting forecasting and control tasks for ground cellular infrastructure. However, training such models is challenged by heterogeneous ground-cell traffic patterns, intermittent links to ground stations, and the satellites' own orbital motion, which continuously shifts the data each satellite observes. In this work, we extend Decentralized Federated Clustering (DFCA) to the LEO setting and apply it to cellular internet-traffic forecasting on the Telecom Italia Milan+Trentino dataset. Satellites cooperate exclusively through $k$-nearest inter-satellite gossip with no ground-side aggregator, while zero-shot head selection lets each satellite specialize to the latent traffic regime of the ground cell currently beneath it. Averaged over $K{=}20$ post-training orbital snapshots, our extension reduces forecasting Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) by $15.3\%$ over a decentralized FedAvg baseline of equivalent capacity, with cluster recovery accuracy of $85.3\%$. The results indicate that clustered specialization yields measurable gains under the structural heterogeneity inherent to realistic cellular-over-LEO scenarios.
  </details>

- **[Assessing the Physical Interpretability of AlphaEarth Foundation Embeddings Through Multi-Sensor Satellite Time-Series Benchmarking for Agricultural Mapping](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34019)**  `arXiv:2611.34019`  
  _El Houcine El Moussaoui, Chouaib El Hachimi, Saïd Khabba, Salwa Belaqziz, Bouchra Ait Hssaine, Abderrahman Lahrouni, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
