  </details>

- **[Reification as a Transferable Vocabulary: Zero-Shot Link Prediction with Vanilla GNNs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11347)**  `arXiv:2609.11347`  
  _Camille Pradel_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Knowledge graph foundation models such as ULTRA achieve zero-shot link prediction on unseen graphs through dedicated architectures that hard-code a transfer mechanism. In this work we move that mechanism out of the architecture and into the representation, by \emph{reifying} the input graph: every fact becomes a node, connected to its subject, object, and relation type through a fixed vocabulary of six meta-relations, with relation types as anonymous shared nodes rather than model parameters. On this representation, five textbook GNNs (GAT, GINE with sum and with mean+max aggregation, GraphSAGE, R-GCN), each trained on a single knowledge graph of 4,245 triples for 30 minutes on one NVIDIA A100, transfer zero-shot to 40 inductive link-prediction benchmarks. The best of them, an off-the-shelf GAT, matches ULTRA, a dedicated foundation model pretrained on three graphs, across ULTRA's own evaluation suite. The same fixed vocabulary extends to relational databases, a row becoming an entity and a foreign-key column a relation type; a preliminary probe on two unseen databases, with no cell values, schema text or in-context labels, shows a model of this family pretrained on three knowledge graphs ranking foreign-key targets far above random-initialization and degree controls. We release the code, the checkpoints, and the evaluation pipeline for all 40 benchmarks.
  </details>

- **[CrevasseSeg: A Label-Efficient UAV Crevasse Segmentation Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15790)**  `arXiv:2608.15790`  
  _Steven Wallace, William D. Harcourt, Richard Hann, Aiden Durrant, Somayajulu Sripada, Georgios Leontidis_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Crevasse mapping from uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) imagery supports glaciological research and field safety, but pixel-level annotation requires costly expert effort. We introduce CrevasseSeg, a binary segmentation evaluation framework from the terminus of Borebreen, Svalbard, comprising 2,244 unlabelled UAV orthomosaic tiles for self-supervised/unsupervised fine-tuning and 200 labelled tiles (24 validation, 176 test). We benchmark five self-supervised objectives (BYOL, Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD), Barlow Twins, VICReg and a combined BYOL-JSD) across O-Net, O-Net++ and a DINOv3-initialised O-Net. Frozen features are read out with a linear probe and an XGBoost classifier, both fit only on the 24 validation tiles. At the final decoder block, the two readouts invert. DINOv3 models are mostly the weakest under linear probing, often collapsing to a constant prediction, yet they are the strongest under XGBoost. This pattern does not hold at earlier decoder blocks. UMAP suggests why: DINOv3 fragments pixels into many small, locally interleaved clusters, whereas the convolutional models embed them on a single class-sorted manifold. Satellite-pretrained DINOv3 beats natural-image initialisation for every objective under XGBoost (+9.7 mDSC on average), but not consistently under linear probing. Our pipeline, DINOv3-ViT-L-Sat-O-Net-BYOL-JSD, reaches 74.75 mDSC / 61.16 mIoU (77.04 / 64.28 with a decoder-block ensemble), on par with BYOL alone, and outperforms RGB-pixel ML baselines. However, a frozen DINOv3-Sat encoder with an XGBoost readout alone reaches 77.18 / 64.17. It matches or exceeds every SSL variant and comes within 0.71 mDSC of a fully supervised DINOv3 U-Net, highlighting satellite foundation models as a strong baseline. We release CrevasseSeg as a benchmark for label-efficient segmentation in remote sensing.
  </details>

- **[ED-DiT: Physics-Guided Diffusion Pretraining for Transferable Molecular Representations from Electron Density](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03260)**  `arXiv:2608.03260`  
  _Shuang Liang, Haocheng Wang, Jiayi Song, Shuquan Ye, Ben Fei_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Pretraining has shown strong potential for learning transferable representations, yet it remains underexplored for electron-density-based molecular learning. Electron density provides a continuous three-dimensional description of molecular electronic structure, capturing both local spatial patterns and global physical quantities. This raises a key question: can electron-density fields be used for self-supervised pretraining to learn a shared representation that transfers across diverse electronic-structure-related tasks? We propose ED-DiT, a physics-guided Diffusion Transformer for self-supervised pretraining on electron-density point clouds. ED-DiT learns reusable representations by reconstructing corrupted and partially masked log-density fields across diffusion noise levels. An electron-number consistency constraint is further introduced to preserve the total electronic mass. The pretrained encoder can be adapted to property prediction, open-/closed-shell classification, molecule-electron-density retrieval, and molecule-conditioned electron-density prediction. Experiments on six EDBench tasks show that ED-DiT consistently outperforms the same architecture trained from scratch, especially under limited supervision. For molecule-conditioned electron-density prediction, it reduces RMSE from 2.2474 to 1.3753 and surpasses the available baseline. With only 10% labels, it improves orbital energy prediction RMSE from 0.0293 to 0.0138. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of physics-guided electron-density pretraining for learning transferable molecular representations.
  </details>

- **[Safe Inference-Time Alignment via Lagrangian Reward Augmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02781)**  `arXiv:2607.02781`  
  _Yaswanth Chittepu, Ativ Joshi, Sohini Chintala, Scott Niekum_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Inference-time alignment steers a frozen language model during decoding using auxiliary reward signals, avoiding the cost of repeated weight updates. However, existing inference-time alignment methods typically optimize a single scalar score, so explicit safety constraints must either be ignored or encoded through manually tuned penalties. We propose Lagrangian Reward Augmentation (LARA), a general inference-time alignment framework under safety constraints. Starting from a KL-regularized constrained objective with a reward model and a cost model, LARA dualizes the constraint and reduces the optimization problem to a one-dimensional convex problem over a nonnegative dual variable. Estimated on a small calibration set, this dual variable defines an augmented reward that can be used as a drop-in scoring signal within existing inference-time alignment methods. For sequence-level sampling methods, such as Best-of-N reranking, the calibrated dual variable corresponds to the solution of the expected-cost constrained problem. For token-level reward-guided decoding methods, the same construction yields a principled dual-calibrated heuristic rather than an exact constrained-policy guarantee. We evaluate LARA on both sequence-level and token-level inference-time alignment methods, and find that LARA improves the helpfulness-harmlessness tradeoff, with Best-of-N achieving the best performance among inference-time methods, approaching finetuning-based direct alignment baselines.
  </details>

- **[The Curse of Multiple Mediators: Hidden Interaction Effects in Activation Patching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27510)**  `arXiv:2606.27510`  
  _Sankaran Vaidyanathan, David Arbour, Aaron Mueller, Scott Niekum, David Jensen_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Activation patching is a primary tool in mechanistic interpretability. It attributes causal responsibility for a model's behavior to each of its individual components by estimating its natural indirect effect (NIE). Re-deriving the activation patching estimand from causal mediation analysis, we find that the NIE does not solely capture the causal effect through the specific component. It also contains interaction effects (INT) that measure how much the component's causal effect itself depends on the states of other components in the model. A natural response may be to try to eliminate INT by adjusting the estimator or unit of analysis, but each of these potential remedies has predictable failure modes. We demonstrate these failure modes in the GPT-2 IOI circuit; components whose causal importance is conditional on the state of other components are either invisible or artificially inflated. We prove that INT scales with the distance between clean and patched component activations, is negligible when the model is nearly affine between them, and decomposes combinatorially into pairwise and higher-order group interactions. Despite its inevitability, INT is not a nuisance to be eliminated, but rather a diagnostic for interpretability studies. Its individual and group-level magnitude and sign signal when causal conclusions are prompt-dependent, and when greedy NIE-based component ranking will miss mechanisms only discoverable through combinatorial search.
  </details>

- **[Sample Where You Struggle: Sharpening Base Model Reasoning via Entropy-Guided Power Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.09926)**  `arXiv:2606.09926`  
  _Hong Guo, Nianhui Guo, Christoph Meinel, Haojin Yang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Sampling from the sequence-level power distribution elicits RL-level reasoning from base language models without any parameter updates, but the standard Metropolis--Hastings (MH), a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampler, is both expensive and slow-mixing. We trace both to a structural mismatch: the power distribution mainly departs from the base distribution at a sparse, spatially clustered set of high-entropy decision points, yet MH proposes resampling positions uniformly along the prefix---wasting compute on near-degenerate conditionals while under-mixing precisely where modes diverge. We propose Entropy-Guided Power Sampling (EGPS), a training-free and verifier-free approximate sampler that re-derives its proposal from token-level entropy already in the forward pass. EGPS skips deterministic blocks, localizes each MCMC move to a high-entropy neighborhood, and applies Multiple-Try Metropolis at decision points---making sampling cost scale with entropy mass rather than sequence length. EGPS targets significant speedup with accuracy that matches or improves on MH power sampling: across three base models and three benchmarks it attains best or tied-best accuracy on 5 of 9 settings; on Qwen2.5-Math-7B it is best or tied-best on all three (MATH500 $75.8\%$, HumanEval $62.2\%$, GPQA $42.4\%$), with wall-clock speedups over the MH baseline of up to $12.6\times$ across these benchmarks. Our code is available atthis https URL
  </details>

- **[A Geometric View for Understanding Concept Learning and Neuron Interpretation in Sparse Autoencoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.07007)**  `arXiv:2606.07007`  
  _Chenhao Zhang, Chris Lin, Xiaojian Chen, Hanqi Feng, Su-In Lee_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We propose a unified mathematical framework for a geometric understanding of concept learning and neuron interpretation in sparse autoencoders (SAEs). While SAEs improve interpretability of neural networks by learning sparse feature representations, a principled definition of ''concept'' and ''learning'' remains unclear. We formalize concepts as sets of data points and cast concept learning as a set-alignment problem between human-defined and model-induced concepts. This formulation distinguishes three increasingly strong notions of learning -- detection, separation, and approximation -- and yields geometric conditions, error bounds, and capacity constraints for when concepts can be represented by individual neurons or multi-neuron units. It also provides a set-theoretic account for common SAE phenomena, including feature splitting, feature absorption, feature families, and hierarchical concepts. Finally, we connect concept learning and neuron interpretation through formal concept analysis, showing that the two directions need not agree and that their many-to-many structure can be organized by concept lattices. Experiments on synthetic data with ReLU and Top-$K$ SAEs illustrate the theory and reveal the effects of SAE size and sparsity on concept learning.
  </details>

- **[Scalable Heterogeneous Graph Foundation Models for Data-Driven Optimal Power Flow in Smart Grids](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23194)**  `arXiv:2605.23194`  
  _Massimiliano Lupo Pasini, Yijiang Li, Kibaek Kim, Teja Kuruganti_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Fast and reliable optimal power flow (OPF) approximation is important for power system operation, yet heterogeneous OPF graph models are often evaluated either with architecture-specific implementations or on limited training corpora. This paper presents a large-scale heterogeneous graph-learning workflow, built on HydraGNN, for data-driven OPF surrogate modeling and graph foundation-model (GFM) development. The workflow preserves buses, generators, loads, shunts, alternating-current (AC) lines, transformers, and device-to-bus relations and provides a common implementation for distributed preprocessing, multi-graphics-processing-unit (GPU) training, hyperparameter optimization (HPO), and downstream adaptation. Using approximately three million heterogeneous graphs from ten Power Grid Library for Benchmarking AC Optimal Power Flow Algorithms (PGLib-OPF) cases spanning 14 to 13,659 buses, we compare six heterogeneous graph neural network (GNN) families under a common HPO campaign on Frontier, resulting in two compact HeteroSAGE and HeteroHEAT models (~1.6-1.7 million parameters) that achieve the lowest observed validation MSE. Strong and weak scaling using up to 1,024 Frontier nodes show that 256 nodes (corresponding to 1,024 AMD MI250X GPUs) provides the best time-to-solution balance for the measured workload. Two downstream tasks evaluate task adaptation on the IEEE 118-bus case: a classification task to distinguish nominal operating conditions from artificially generated extreme-overload conditions and N-1 single-component-outage regression to predict bus voltage magnitude and phase angle. Partial fine-tuning provides the strongest balance between predictive performance and computational requirements.
  </details>

- **[The Transformer as a Polar State Estimator](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11007)**  `arXiv:2605.11007`  
  _Peter Racioppo_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We show that the core components of the Transformer---attention, residual connections, normalization, and rotary encodings---arise from a single state-estimation problem. We treat each token as a noisy reading of a rotating direction on the hypersphere, taken at its own magnitude. Estimating this direction unifies the architecture: rotational dynamics give rotary encodings, robust estimation gives attention, normalization enforces the spherical geometry, and the residual connection steps toward the estimate. This reconciles normalized queries and keys with unnormalized values as opposite assumptions on whether token magnitudes are independent or share a common scale. Finally, the \emph{Polar Transformer} restores three elements standard blocks drop: rotating values alongside keys, using key magnitudes as confidence, and stepping toward the estimate rather than adding it.
  </details>

- **[Regret-Oracle Complexity Tradeoffs in Agnostic Online Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.07155)**  `arXiv:2605.07155`  
  _Idan Attias, Steve Hanneke, Arvind Ramaswami_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Agnostic online learning is classically solved via a reduction to the realizable setting, utilizing Littlestone's Standard Optimal Algorithm (SOA) as a base learner. However, the SOA can be computationally intractable to implement even for a single round. To overcome this barrier, recent work in oracle-efficient online learning replaces the SOA with a realizable base learner that accesses the concept class exclusively through an offline empirical risk minimization (ERM) oracle. While such agnostic learners achieve expected regret $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\big(\sqrt{T\cdot 2^{\mathcal{O}(d_{\mathrm{LD}})}}\big)$, which is near-optimal in the horizon $T$ for fixed Littlestone dimension $d_{\mathrm{LD}}$, they require $\mathcal{O}\big(T^{2^{\mathcal{O}(d_{\mathrm{LD}})}}\big)$ oracle calls. In this work, we significantly improve this oracle complexity while relying on an even weaker primitive: a weak-consistency oracle, which merely decides whether a given labeled dataset is realizable. At the core of our approach is an adaptive and dynamic agnostic-to-realizable reduction that actively prunes non-realizable label sequences on the fly. By using the VC dimension ($d_{\mathrm{VC}}$) to bound the number of dynamically maintained active paths, our algorithm reduces the total query complexity down to $\mathcal{O}(T^{d_{\mathrm{VC}}+1})$ while perfectly preserving near-optimal expected regret. Crucially, this dynamic pruning also yields a memory reduction over the standard reduction. Furthermore, we formally quantify the regret--oracle complexity tradeoff, providing upper bounds that smoothly interpolate between restricted query budgets and attainable expected regret. We complement these with lower bounds proving that any learner restricted to $Q = o(\sqrt{T})$ queries must suffer an expected regret of $\Omega(T/Q)$.
  </details>

- **[EEG Foundation Models Need Channel Adaptation, but Fixed Channel Mappings Often Suffice](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.23091)**  `arXiv:2604.23091`  
  _Kuntal Kokate, Dung Truong, Pierre Guetschel, Bruno Aristimunha, Arnaud Delorme_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Scaling EEG foundation models requires pooling data across heterogeneous montages, so every model needs a channel-adaptation step mapping an arbitrary source montage onto its expected input. Whether this step must be learned, and whether it confounds cross-model comparison, is untested. We compare five channel-adaptation routes (a learned Conv1d projection, spherical spline interpolation, source-space decomposition, Riemannian re-centering, and each model's native handling) across five pretrained models (5M--157M parameters), five downstream tasks, two training regimes, and up to 15 random seeds. The answer is architecture-dependent rather than adapter-universal: fixed or native mappings are best in 18 of 25 model--task cells, but regime-specific wins are distributed across Native/Conv1d/SSI/OmnEEG/Riemannian. Rigid fixed-input BENDR is the main case where a learned bridge is needed; the strongest model, CBraMod, reaches its best results without adding a learned channel adapter. Because a learned adapter adds a montage-dependent task parameter budget, we recommend reporting frozen-probe benchmarks under a fixed/native route, and treating learned adapters in full fine-tuning as part of the model being evaluated. Source code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Benchmarking LLM-Based Investment Advisor Agents for Asset Allocation in the Chinese ETF Market: Overview of NLPCC 2026 Shared Task 4](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.22305)**  `arXiv:2603.22305`  
  _Liyuan Chen, Shilong Li, Jiangpeng Yan, Shuoling Liu, Xi Cheng, Haoran Zhang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large Language Models (LLMs) convert unstructured financial news into actionable trading strategies, yet standardized end-to-end benchmarks tailored for Chinese market remain scarce. We select common Chinese Exchange-Traded Funds (ETFs) as the investment universe and introduce CN-Buzz2Portfolio, the official benchmark of NLPCC 2026 Shared Task 4. Investment agents take daily trending Chinese financial news and historical ETF price-volume series as inputs to complete news filtering, news-to-ETF mapping and risk-controlled portfolio construction. To facilitate fair comparison, we provide a reproducible Compression--Perception--Allocation baseline compatible with mainstream LLMs. The task contains two ETF allocation tracks: Macro-Asset Allocation and Sector-Rotation Allocation. We adopt chronological data split across 2024--2026 to alleviate overfitting, with final rankings determined by out-of-sample Sharpe ratios on unseen test data. 26 teams registered for the task, and 14 submitted self-designed agent systems. Three core findings emerge: (1) Native LLM reasoning capability cannot translate to superior investment returns, as models show highly differentiated risk-return characteristics; (2) Hybrid frameworks are widely adopted, where LLMs extract textual semantic signals and quantitative modules incorporate price-volume factors and risk constraints; (3) Systems based on identical base LLMs yield distinct results with different signal processing, memory and portfolio construction modules. The project is publicly released atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Thinking Deeper, Not Longer: Memory-Efficient Latent Chain-of-Thought with Depth-Recurrent Transformers for Compositional Generalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.21676)**  `arXiv:2603.21676`  
  _Hung-Hsuan Chen_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Standard Transformers have a fixed computational depth, limiting their ability to generalize to tasks that require variable-depth reasoning. The usual remedy, Chain-of-Thought (CoT), spends tokens to reason, inflating the key--value cache, so memory becomes the limiting cost when reasoning is served over large query batches. We study a depth-recurrent Transformer that decouples computational depth from parameter count by iterating a shared-weight block, so that adding reasoning steps leaves peak inference memory unchanged and grows latency only linearly, with no token generation. Three ingredients support the recurrence over 20+ thinking steps: a silent thinking objective that supervises only the final output, LayerScale initialization, and an identity-biased gate that opens a gradient highway across steps. We characterize it on three compositional domains with decreasing structural bias: graph reachability (adjacency masking), nested boolean logic (relative positioning), and unstructured relational text (no structural positional cue). We find a \emph{computational frontier}: accuracy climbs once the thinking-step count meets the task's complexity, reaching near-perfect performance on the two structured tasks and a lower plateau on unstructured text. How it climbs depends on the structural bias---abruptly from chance on the graph task, gradually on the other two. Depth recurrence extrapolates beyond the training range: it succeeds on the graph task where fixed-depth models barely extrapolate, and on the two sequence tasks comes within two points of fixed-depth Transformers that use $4$--$6.4\times$ more parameters. On the graph task, whose adjacency mask makes propagation depth verifiable, intermediate per-step supervision---a standard recipe for deep iterative models---consistently \emph{harms} this extrapolation at widths $d \geq 256$. We release the code for reproducibility.
  </details>

- **[Manifold-Matching Autoencoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.16568)**  `arXiv:2603.16568`  
  _Laurent Cheret, Vincent Létourneau, Isar Nejadgholi, Chris Drummond, Hussein Al Osman, Maia Fraser_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Manipulating the structure of data in the latent space of an autoencoder is a long-standing goal of representation learning. We propose a simple regularization, Manifold Matching, that imposes an explicit geometric structure on that latent space. The idea is to take a reference representation R of the data, which need not be the raw input X fed to the network, and to minimize, batch-wise, the mean squared error between the pairwise distances in R and those in the latent space Z. Although the autoencoder still learns to reconstruct X, the shape of its latent space comes to mimic that of R. The objective requires no labels, only reference distances, and because those are scalars, the dimensionality of R is decoupled from that of Z: any reference can guide any bottleneck. Using this single instrument we study how different geometric structures can be imposed on a latent space, comparing against autoencoders built on geometric or topological regularizers. Across fifteen datasets under a shared protocol with statistical testing, the resulting Manifold-Matching Autoencoder (MMAE) matches the global-structure quality of persistence-based autoencoders, statistically tying RTD-AE on distance correlation and triplet accuracy, and stays competitive on the local and topological metrics that other methods lead, at the computational cost of a plain autoencoder: it uses only a batched distance loss, with no persistence computation. We frame MMAE not as a universal winner but as an efficient and controllable regularizer whose reference selects which structure the latent inherits, and which turns any fixed embedding into a reusable out-of-sample encoder. All experiments use a two-dimensional bottleneck.
  </details>

- **[FairMed-XGB: A Bayesian-Optimised Multi-Metric Framework with Explainability for Demographic Equity in Critical Healthcare Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.14947)**  `arXiv:2603.14947`  
  _Mitul Goswami, Romit Chatterjee, Arif Ahmed Sekh_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Background:Machine learning models in emergency medicine often exhibit demographic biases, particularly gender disparities, which can compromise fairness, clinical trust, and decision-making reliability. Existing mitigation approaches typically optimise isolated fairness metrics, failing to address the multi-dimensional nature of bias while maintaining predictive performance and interpretability. Methods: We propose FairMed-XGB, a Bayesian-optimised, multi-metric fairness framework integrated into an XGBoost classifier. The model incorporates a composite fairness-aware loss function combining Statistical Parity Difference, Theil Index, and Wasserstein Distance. Bayesian optimisation is used to balance fairness and predictive accuracy. The framework is evaluated on seven cohorts derived from the MIMIC-IV-ED and eICU datasets. SHAP-based explainability is employed to analyse feature contributions and identify bias-related patterns. Results: FairMed-XGB significantly reduces gender-based disparities across all cohorts. Statistical Parity Difference decreases by 40-51% on MIMIC-IV-ED and 10-19% on eICU datasets. Theil Index values reduce by four to five orders of magnitude, approaching near-zero levels, while Wasserstein Distance decreases by 20-72%. These improvements are achieved with minimal impact on predictive performance (AUC-ROC reduction <0.02). SHAP analysis demonstrates reduced dependence on gender-proxy features and improved distributional fairness. Conclusions: FairMed-XGB provides a robust and interpretable framework for mitigating demographic bias in emergency medicine prediction models. By jointly optimising multiple fairness objectives and preserving model performance, it enables equitable and trustworthy AI deployment in high-stakes clinical settings. The integration of explainability further supports transparency and clinical adoption.
  </details>

- **[SVDP: Training-Free Contextual Sparsity Predictors for Fast LLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.14110)**  `arXiv:2603.14110`  
  _Georgii Serbin, Kirill Koshkin, Zhongao Sun, Anastasiya Bistrigova, C.C. Korikov_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Contextual sparsity is one of the approaches used to reduce computational complexity in the inference process of large language models (LLMs). Existing techniques for efficient LLM inference acceleration based on contextual sparsity with minimal accuracy degradation require training sparse pattern predictors. This paper presents a framework for accelerating inference of ReGLU-based feed-forward networks (FFNs) within LLMs. The proposed framework provides a fast, training-free method for building sparse pattern predictors using truncation-aware singular value decomposition (SVD) of the gate projection matrix, along with a threshold calibration algorithm, and inference executors supporting conditional computation on CUDA and CANN devices. Experiments on three sparse LLMs with an average activation sparsity level of 90% in the FFNs demonstrate up to a 1.8x reduction in end-to-end decoding time while maintaining less than 1% degradation in benchmark scores on tasks involving complex math and code generation. This work advances the deployment of LLMs on edge devices.
  </details>

- **[Localized Dynamics-Aware Domain Adaptation for Off-Dynamics Offline Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21072)**  `arXiv:2602.21072`  
  _Zhangjie Xia, Yu Yang, Pan Xu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Off-dynamics offline reinforcement learning (RL) aims to learn a policy for a target domain using limited target data and abundant source data collected under different transition dynamics. Existing methods typically address dynamics mismatch either globally over the state space or via pointwise data filtering; these approaches can miss localized cross-domain similarities or incur high computational cost. We propose Localized Dynamics-Aware Domain Adaptation (LoDADA), which exploits localized dynamics mismatch to better reuse source data. LoDADA clusters transitions from source and target datasets and estimates cluster-level dynamics discrepancy via domain discrimination. Source transitions from clusters with small discrepancy are more likely to be retained compared with those from clusters with large discrepancy. This yields a fine-grained and scalable data selection strategy that avoids overly coarse global assumptions and expensive per-sample filtering. We provide theoretical insights and extensive experiments across environments with diverse global and local dynamics shifts. Results show that LoDADA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art off-dynamics offline RL methods by better leveraging localized distribution mismatch.
  </details>

- **[In- and Out-of-Distribution Generalization of Reasoning in Multimodal LLMs for Simple Visual Planning Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.15460)**  `arXiv:2602.15460`  
  _Yannic Neuhaus, Chanoknan Tanchotikul, Nicolas Flammarion, Matthias Hein, Francesco Croce_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Integrating reasoning in (multimodal) large language models has recently led to significant improvement of their capabilities. However, generalization in reasoning models is still vaguely defined and poorly understood. In this work, we present an evaluation framework to rigorously examine how well chain-of-thought (CoT) approaches generalize in simple visual planning, specifically on a grid-based navigation task. The versatility of the task and its data allows us to fine-tune model variants using different input representations (visual and textual) and CoT reasoning strategies, and systematically evaluate them under both in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) test conditions. Our experiments show that the out-of-distribution generalization (e.g., to larger maps) is largely impacted by the format used for input maps and CoT chains. Surprisingly, we find that coordinate-based reasoning traces which combine text descriptions yield the best OOD generalization. Moreover, CoT reproducing the steps of the A* algorithm yields the state-of-the-art ID accuracy, and simple augmentation of the map solutions seen during training greatly boosts OOD results. Repeating the experiments with maps represented by coordinates yields similar results for another model family. Tests on structurally complex maps reveal a sharp performance drop when shortest solutions require many movement directions or turns. Additional fine-tuning on examples of directionally complex maps substantially recovers this performance. Finally, purely text-based models consistently outperform those utilizing image-based inputs, including a recently proposed approach relying on latent space reasoning.
  </details>

- **[Explainable Machine-Learning based Detection of Knee Injuries in Runners](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11668)**  `arXiv:2602.11668`  
  _David Fuentes-Jiménez, Sara García-de-Villa, David Casillas-Pérez, Pablo Floría, Francisco-Manuel Melgarejo-Meseguer_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Running is a widely practiced activity but shows a high incidence of knee injuries, especially Patellofemoral Pain Syndrome (PFPS) and Iliotibial Band Syndrome (ITBS). Identifying gait patterns linked to these injuries can improve clinical decision-making, which requires precise systems capable of capturing and analyzing temporal kinematic data.This study uses optical motion capture systems to enhance detection of injury-related running patterns. We analyze a public dataset of 839 treadmill recordings from healthy and injured runners to evaluate how effectively these systems capture dynamic parameters relevant to injury classification. The focus is on the stance phase, using joint and segment angle time series and discrete point values.Three classification tasks are addressed: healthy vs. injured, healthy vs. PFPS, and healthy vs. ITBS. We examine different feature spaces, from traditional point-based metrics to full stance-phase time series and hybrid representations. Multiple models are tested, including classical algorithms (K-Nearest Neighbors, Gaussian Processes, Decision Trees) and deep learning architectures (CNNs, LSTMs).Performance is evaluated with accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. Explainability tools such as Shapley values, saliency maps, and Grad-CAM are used to interpret model behavior. Results show that combining time series with point values substantially improves detection. Deep learning models outperform classical ones, with CNNs achieving the highest accuracy: 77.9% for PFPS, 73.8% for ITBS, and 71.43% for the combined injury class.These findings highlight the potential of motion capture systems coupled with advanced machine learning to identify knee injury-related running patterns.
  </details>

- **[TopoPrune: Robust Data Pruning via Unified Latent Space Topology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.02739)**  `arXiv:2602.02739`  
  _Arjun Roy, Prajna G. Malettira, Manish Nagaraj, Kaushik Roy_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Geometric data pruning methods, while practical for leveraging pretrained models, are fundamentally unstable. Their reliance on extrinsic geometry renders them highly sensitive to latent space perturbations, causing performance to degrade during cross-architecture transfer or in the presence of feature noise. We introduce TopoPrune, a framework which resolves this challenge by leveraging topology to capture the stable, intrinsic structure of data. TopoPrune operates at two scales, (1) utilizing a topology-aware manifold approximation to establish a global low-dimensional embedding of the dataset. Subsequently, (2) it employs differentiable persistent homology to perform a local topological optimization on the manifold embeddings, ranking samples by their structural complexity. We demonstrate that our unified dual-scale topological approach ensures high accuracy and precision, particularly at significant dataset pruning rates (e.g., 90%). Furthermore, through the inherent stability properties of topology, TopoPrune is (a) exceptionally robust to noise perturbations of latent feature embeddings and (b) demonstrates superior transferability across diverse network architectures. This study demonstrates a promising avenue towards stable and principled topology-based frameworks for robust data-efficient learning.
  </details>

- **[Latent Diffusion for Internet of Things Attack Data Generation in Intrusion Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.16976)**  `arXiv:2601.16976`  
  _Estela Sánchez-Carballo, Francisco M. Melgarejo-Meseguer, José Luis Rojo-Álvarez_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The growing deployment of IoT systems has increased the need for reliable intrusion detection under heterogeneous and imbalanced network traffic. However, representative malicious traffic, particularly for underrepresented attacks, remains difficult to obtain, while existing generative approaches do not consistently preserve distributional fidelity, multivariate dependencies, and coverage simultaneously. This work proposes LaDIS, an attack-specific framework that learns a mixed-type autoencoder representation and performs diffusion in an adaptive continuous latent space. LaDIS was compared with established adversarial, variational, and direct-space diffusion approaches across representative Flooding, Botnet, Recon, and Stealthy attacks using complementary measures of marginal and multivariate fidelity, dependency preservation, real--synthetic distinguishability, manifold structure, and computational efficiency. LaDIS provided a competitive balance across these dimensions, with particularly strong results for representative Botnet, Recon, and Stealthy attacks, while revealing an attack-dependent fidelity--coverage trade-off. Performing diffusion in latent space also reduced sampling time by approximately 3--5 times relative to direct-space diffusion, with negligible decoding overhead. Downstream utility was evaluated using TabNet and XGBoost, demonstrating that partial LaDIS augmentation consistently produced the best performance, increasing balanced accuracy from 0.86 to 0.94 for TabNet and from 0.92 to 0.96 for XGBoost, while improving the F1-score for low-volume attack families from 0.73 to 0.84 and from 0.82 to 0.88, respectively. These results show that attack-adaptive latent diffusion can generate structurally faithful attack traffic efficiently and, when used selectively, improve intrusion detection for underrepresented attacks.
  </details>

- **[Neural Isomorphic Fields: A Transformer-based Algebraic Numerical Embedding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.12095)**  `arXiv:2601.12095`  
  _Hamidreza Sadeghi, Saeedeh Momtazi, Reza Safabakhsh_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Neural network models often face challenges when processing very small or very large numbers due to issues such as overflow, underflow, and unstable output variations. To mitigate these problems, we propose using embedding vectors for numbers instead of directly using their raw values. These embeddings aim to retain essential algebraic properties while preventing numerical instabilities. We introduce Neural Isomorphic Fields (NIF), a digit-sequence Transformer autoencoder trained with two learned commutative operators and an antisymmetric neural comparator. At zero loss, the embeddings provably form an ordered integral domain isomorphic to the decimal fractions, whose field of fractions is isomorphic to the rationals. For the trained model, we bound errors of operations, chains and algebraic laws by decoding margins, defects and Lipschitz constants. Trained on up to 25 digits, NIF reaches at least 99.9% exact match on closure, identity, associativity and distributivity and 99.8% on ten-step chains and the order relation. With four channels per decimal place, reconstruction and both operations exceed 99.7% exact match on numbers of up to 200 digits whose parts stay within training lengths, so the dimension grows linearly. In a language model, frozen operators raise exact match on 14-20-digit word problems from 12.0% (operators off) to 39.7%.
  </details>

- **[Learning with Limited Antigenic Labels: Semi-supervised Prediction of Influenza A Antigenic Relationships with Protein Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.05222)**  `arXiv:2512.05222`  
  _Yanhua Xu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Influenza A viruses (IAVs) undergo frequent antigenic changes that require regular vaccine updates. Because haemagglutination inhibition (HI) assays are labour-intensive, antigenic measurements remain limited relative to the available sequence data. We combined pre-trained protein representations with semi-supervised learning (SSL) to predict antigenic relationships when labelled data are scarce. HA1 sequences from H1N1, H3N2, H5N1, and H9N2 were encoded using ESM-2, ProtVec, ProtT5, and ProtBert. Using these embeddings, we compared self-training and label spreading with supervised baselines, including random forest (RF) and support vector machine (SVM) models. Nested cross-validation evaluated performance with 25%, 50%, 75%, or 100% of training labels retained. Self-training slightly improved RF performance in most settings but generally reduced SVM's ability to distinguish antigenically similar from antigenically different virus pairs. With 25% of training labels retained, self-training increased mean macro-F1 from 0.791 to 0.798 for ProtVec-RF and from 0.776 to 0.778 for ESM-2 RF. Label spreading performed best with ProtVec but remained below supervised RF across all protein representations and training-label proportions. In supervised and self-training RF models using ESM-2 or ProtBert, additional training labels improved classification of H3N2 antigenic relationships, whereas H9N2 remained the most difficult subtype. RF frequently misclassified antigenically similar H9N2 pairs as variants.
  </details>

- **[Network of Theseus (like the ship)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.04198)**  `arXiv:2512.04198`  
  _Vighnesh Subramaniam, Colin Conwell, Boris Katz, Andrei Barbu, Brian Cheung_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  A standard assumption in deep learning is that the inductive bias introduced by a neural network architecture must persist from training through inference. The architecture you train with is the architecture you deploy. This assumption constrains the community from selecting architectures that may have desirable efficiency or design properties due to difficulties with optimization. We challenge this assumption with the Network of Theseus (NoT), a method for progressively converting a trained, or even untrained, guide network architecture part-by-part into an entirely different target network architecture while preserving the performance of the guide network. At each stage, components in the guide network architecture are incrementally replaced with the target architecture modules and aligned via representational similarity metrics. This procedure preserves most of the functionality of the guide network even under substantial architectural changes-for example, converting a convolutional network into a multilayer perceptron, or GPT-2 into a recurrent neural network. By decoupling optimization from deployment, NoT expands the space of viable inference-time architectures, opening opportunities for better accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs and enabling more directed exploration of the architectural design space.
  </details>

- **[ML-Tool-Bench: Tool-Augmented Planning for ML Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.00672)**  `arXiv:2512.00672`  
  _Yaswanth Chittepu, Raghavendra Addanki, Tung Mai, Anup Rao, Branislav Kveton_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The development of autonomous machine learning (ML) agents capable of end-to-end data science workflows represents a significant frontier in artificial intelligence. These agents must orchestrate complex sequences of data analysis, feature engineering, model selection, and hyperparameter optimization, tasks that require sophisticated planning and iteration. While recent work on building ML agents has explored using large language models (LLMs) for direct code generation, tool-augmented approaches offer greater modularity and reliability. However, existing tool-use benchmarks focus primarily on task-specific tool selection or argument extraction for tool invocation, failing to evaluate the sophisticated planning capabilities required for ML Agents. In this work, we introduce a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating tool-augmented ML agents using a curated set of 61 specialized tools and 15 tabular ML challenges from Kaggle. Our benchmark goes beyond traditional tool-use evaluation by incorporating an in-memory named object management, allowing agents to flexibly name, save, and retrieve intermediate results throughout the workflows. We demonstrate that standard ReAct-style approaches struggle to generate valid tool sequences for complex ML pipelines, and that tree search methods with LLM-based evaluation underperform due to inconsistent state scoring. To address these limitations, we propose two simple approaches: 1) using shaped deterministic rewards with structured textual feedback, and 2) decomposing the original problem into a sequence of sub-tasks, which significantly improves trajectory validity and task performance. Using GPT-4o, our approach improves over ReAct by 16.52 percentile positions, taking the median across all Kaggle challenges. We believe our work provides a foundation for developing more capable tool-augmented planning ML agents.
  </details>

- **[ELBO$_{\mathrm{TDS}}$: Temporal Distribution Shift Generalization for Industry-Scale Recommender Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.21032)**  `arXiv:2511.21032`  
  _Yuxuan Zhu, Cong Fu, Yabo Ni, Anxiang Zeng, Yuan Fang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Temporal distribution shift (TDS) degrades the generalization of recommender systems: models trained on past interactions face systematically different user behavior in future time windows. While incremental training on recent data is widely used in industrial production, it can over-adapt to transient patterns and exacerbate instability. Existing approaches such as invariant learning and self-supervised learning offer partial solutions but often suffer from unstable temporal generalization, representation collapse, or inefficient data utilization. To address these limitations, we propose ELBO$_{\mathrm{TDS}}$, a probabilistic framework for temporally robust recommendation. First, we identify key shifting factors in real-world production data and design a simple yet effective data augmentation strategy that simulates realistic time-varying factors and expands the training support. Second, we derive a self-supervised variational objective, ELBO$_{\mathrm{TDS}}$, to harness the benefits of this extended distribution while preventing representation collapse. Extensive experiments on both a public benchmark and a large-scale industrial dataset demonstrate that ELBO$_{\mathrm{TDS}}$ consistently improves next-period ranking performance over strong baselines. It achieves a 2.33\% uplift in GMV per user in online experiments and has been successfully deployed in production. Code is available atthis https URL
  </details>

- **[Analysis of Variational Sparse Autoencoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.22994)**  `arXiv:2509.22994`  
  _Zachary Baker, Yuxiao Li_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Variational sparse autoencoders (vSAEs) replace a sparse autoencoder's deterministic Top-K mechanism with a sampled Gaussian posterior hypothesized to produce a more robust feature dictionary. To test this, we build permutation comparisons over training seeds for custom analyses, and score two popular benchmarks on one pair of existing checkpoints. When fixing the unit variance and ablating sampling on the vSAE, we find that the gap between the non-sampled vSAE and a Top-K SAE with an L2 activation penalty can be decomposed completely into a set of five implementation details. When we enable sampling and allow the network to learn its own variance, we find that the discrete selection process of Top-K fails when in conjunction with stochastic sampling methods. At the noise scale these models are trained upon, vastly different Top-K feature sets (Jaccard 0.075-0.29, chance 0.067) are found on equal model activations due only to the sampling noise, in two forward passes of one trained model on the same token. Soft methods such as JumpReLU fail to hold their sparsity target as well due to sampling, though under different failure modes. Noise moves its achieved sparsity, and at matched sparsity reconstruction fails to track selection stability (r = -0.55). Ablating the KL loss term recovers only 3.9 percent of the lost reconstruction. The rest is due to sampling.
  </details>

- **[GDS Agent for Graph Algorithmic Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.20637)**  `arXiv:2508.20637`  
  _Borun Shi, Lusine Adunts, Ioannis Panagiotas_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable multimodal information processing and reasoning ability. When equipped with tools through function calling and enhanced with retrieval-augmented techniques, compound LLM-based systems can access closed data sources and answer questions about them. However, they still struggle to process and reason over large-scale graph-structure data. In this technical report we introduce the GDS (Graph Data Science) agent. The GDS agent introduces a comprehensive set of graph algorithms as tools, together with preprocessing (retrieval) and postprocessing of algorithm results, in a model context protocol (MCP) server. It is accompanied by a skill that guides the LLM through graph analysis. The agent can be used with any modern LLM out-of-the-box. GDS agent allows users to ask any question that implicitly and intrinsically requires graph algorithmic reasoning about their data, and quickly obtain accurate and grounded answers. We introduce new benchmarks that evaluate intermediate tool calls as well as final responses, and the results indicate that the GDS agent solves a wide spectrum of graph tasks. We also demonstrate how the GDS agent can perform open-ended analyses at the level of domain experts, on tasks such as money laundering tracing and pattern mining in biology. Finally, we discuss the remaining challenges and the future roadmap.
  </details>

- **[SACA: Selective Attention-Based Clustering Algorithm](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.17150)**  `arXiv:2508.17150`  
  _Meysam Shirdel Bilehsavar, Razieh Ghaedi, Christian O'Reilly_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Clustering algorithms are fundamental tools across many fields, with density-based methods offering particular advantages in identifying arbitrarily shaped clusters and handling noise. However, their effectiveness is often limited by the requirement of critical parameter tuning by users, which typically requires significant domain expertise. This paper introduces a novel density-based clustering algorithm loosely inspired by the concept of selective attention, designed to minimize reliance on parameter tuning for most applications. The proposed method computes an adaptive threshold to exclude sparsely distributed points and outliers, constructs an initial cluster framework, and subsequently reintegrates the filtered points to refine the final results. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmark datasets demonstrate the robustness, accuracy, and ease of use of the proposed approach, establishing it as a powerful alternative to conventional density-based clustering techniques.
  </details>

- **[PLAICraft: Large-Scale Time-Aligned Vision-Speech-Action Dataset for Embodied AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.12707)**  `arXiv:2505.12707`  
  _Yingchen He, Christian D. Weilbach, Martyna E. Wojciechowska, Yiyuan Sun, Jason Yoo, Yuxuan Zhang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Advances in deep generative modeling have made it increasingly plausible to train human-level embodied agents. Yet progress has been limited by the absence of large-scale, real-time, multi-modal, and socially interactive datasets that reflect the sensory-motor complexity of natural environments. To address this, we present PLAICraft, a novel data collection platform and dataset capturing multiplayer Minecraft interactions across five time-aligned modalities: video, game output audio, microphone input audio, mouse, and keyboard actions. Each modality is logged with millisecond time precision, enabling the study of synchronous, embodied behaviour in a rich, open-ended world. The dataset comprises 5525 hours of interactive gameplay from more than 232 participants. Alongside the dataset, we provide an evaluation suite for benchmarking model capabilities in object recognition, spatial awareness, language grounding, and long-term memory. PLAICraft opens a path toward training and evaluating agents that act fluently and purposefully in real time, paving the way for truly embodied artificial intelligence.
  </details>

- **[Improving regional weather forecasts with neural interpolation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.12040)**  `arXiv:2505.12040`  
  _James Jackaman, Oliver Sutton_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  In this paper we design a neural interpolation operator to improve the boundary data for regional weather models, which is a challenging problem as we are required to map multi-scale dynamics between grid resolutions. In particular, we expose a methodology for approaching the problem through the study of a simplified model, with a view to generalise the results in this work to the dynamical core of regional weather models. Our approach will exploit a combination of techniques from image super-resolution with convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and residual networks, in addition to building the flow of atmospheric dynamics into the neural network. We find that building in the flow more than halves the squared error of small networks.
  </details>

- **[Out-of-Distribution Detection on Graphs: A Survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.08105)**  `arXiv:2502.08105`  
  _Tingyi Cai, Yunliang Jiang, Yixin Liu, Zhonglong Zheng, Changqin Huang, Ming Li, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Graph learning has advanced prediction and discovery across a wide range of relational data applications. In evolving environments, new categories and changes in attributes or relationships can produce out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs on which models make confident but unreliable predictions. Graph out-of-distribution (GOOD) detection identifies such nodes or graphs to support rejection and further assessment. This paper presents the first systematic survey dedicated to GOOD detection. We clarify the problem settings and organize existing methods into six categories according to their primary OOD discrimination mechanisms. The review examines their technical connections, supervision and reference requirements, and conditions of use, alongside representative datasets, OOD constructions, benchmarks, and evaluation metrics. Controlled synthetic comparisons deepen the understanding of detection settings by illustrating how representative methods respond to different distribution shifts and graph conditions. We discuss open challenges and outline future research directions, aiming to provide a common foundation for advancing GOOD detection.
  </details>

- **[Forget Vectors at Play: Universal Input Perturbations Driving Machine Unlearning in Image Classification and Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.16780)**  `arXiv:2412.16780`  
  _Changchang Sun, Ren Wang, Yihua Zhang, Jinghan Jia, Jiancheng Liu, Gaowen Liu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Machine unlearning (MU), which seeks to erase the influence of specific unwanted data from already-trained models, is becoming increasingly vital in model editing, particularly to comply with evolving data regulations like the "right to be forgotten". Conventional MU approaches are predominantly model-based, typically requiring retraining or fine-tuning the model's weights to meet unlearning requirements. In this work, we approach the MU problem from an input perturbation-based perspective, where the model weights remain intact throughout the unlearning process. We demonstrate the existence of a proactive input-based unlearning strategy, referred to forget vector, which can be generated as an input-agnostic data perturbation and remains as effective as model-based approximate unlearning approaches in both image classification and image generation. For image classification, we demonstrate that forget vector can induce effective class-wise and random data forgetting in frozen classifiers while preserving performance on retained data. We also explore forget vector arithmetic, whereby multiple class-specific forget vectors can be combined through simple operations (e.g., linear combinations) to generate new forget vectors for unseen unlearning tasks, such as forgetting arbitrary subsets across classes. For image generation, we extend forget vector to conditional diffusion models by jointly perturbing the noisy input and conditioning embeddings of frozen denoisers, enabling targeted removal of unwanted classes and concepts from generated outputs. Extensive experiments on both image classification and image generation validate the effectiveness and adaptability of the forget vector, showcasing its competitive performance relative to state-of-the-art model-based methods while achieving superior parameter efficiency.
  </details>

- **[Caravan MultiMet: Extending Caravan with Multiple Weather Nowcasts and Forecasts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.09459)**  `arXiv:2411.09459`  
  _Guy Shalev, Frederik Kratzert_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The Caravan large-sample hydrology dataset (Kratzert et al., 2023) was created to standardize and harmonize streamflow data from various regional datasets, combined with globally available meteorological forcing and catchment attributes. This community-driven project also allows researchers to conveniently extend the dataset for additional basins, as done 6 times to date (seethis https URL). We present a novel extension to Caravan, focusing on enriching the meteorological forcing data. Our extension adds three precipitation nowcast products (CPC, IMERG v07 Early, and CHIRPS) and three weather forecast products (ECMWF IFS HRES, GraphCast, and CHIRPS-GEFS) to the existing ERA5-Land reanalysis data. The inclusion of diverse data sources, particularly weather forecasts, enables more robust evaluation and benchmarking of hydrological models, especially for real-time forecasting scenarios. To the best of our knowledge, this extension makes Caravan the first large-sample hydrology dataset to incorporate weather forecast data, significantly enhancing its capabilities and fostering advancements in hydrological research, benchmarking, and real-time hydrologic forecasting. The data is publicly available under a CC-BY-4.0 license on Zenodo in two parts (this https URL,this https URL) and on Google Cloud Platform (GCP) - see more under the Data Availability chapter.
  </details>

- **[Tensor Networks Meet Neural Networks: A Survey and Future Perspectives](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.09019)**  `arXiv:2302.09019`  
  _Maolin Wang, Yu Pan, Zenglin Xu, Guangxi Li, Xiangli Yang, Danilo Mandic, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Tensor networks (TNs) and neural networks (NNs) are two fundamental data modeling approaches. TNs were introduced to solve the curse of dimensionality in large-scale tensors by converting an exponential number of dimensions to polynomial complexity. As a result, they have attracted significant attention in the fields of quantum physics and machine learning. Meanwhile, NNs have displayed exceptional performance in various applications, e.g., computer vision, natural language processing, and robotics research. Interestingly, although these two types of networks originate from different observations, they are inherently linked through the typical multilinearity structure underlying both TNs and NNs, thereby motivating a significant number of developments regarding combinations of TNs and NNs. In this paper, we refer to these combinations as tensorial neural networks~(TNNs) and present an introduction to TNNs from both data processing and model architecture perspectives. From the data perspective, we explore the capabilities of TNNs in multi-source fusion, multimodal pooling, data compression, multi-task training, and quantum data processing. From the model perspective, we examine TNNs' integration with various architectures, including Convolutional Neural Networks, Recurrent Neural Networks, Graph Neural Networks, Transformers, Large Language Models, and Quantum Neural Networks. Furthermore, this survey also explores methods for improving TNNs, examines flexible toolboxes for implementing TNNs, and documents TNN development while highlighting potential future directions. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive survey that bridges the connections among NNs and TNs. We provide a curated list of TNNs atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Machine Learning-Driven Virtual Bidding with Electricity Market Efficiency Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.02754)**  `arXiv:2104.02754`  
  _Yinglun Li, Nanpeng Yu, Wei Wang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>

- **[Energy-Aware Distributed Task Allocation via Local Submodular Maximization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34293)**  `arXiv:2611.34293`  
  _Jing Liu, Fangfei Li, Xin Jin, Yang Tang, Ruggero Carli, Luca Ballotta_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  This paper studies distributed task allocation under time-varying agent sets, task sets, and communication graphs. At each decision epoch, the stage allocation problem is formulated as monotone submodular maximization over a time-varying, energy-filtered admissible ground set subject to a partition-matroid constraint. We develop a Distributed Adaptive Greedy Bidding Algorithm (DAGBA) that combines local admissible-set construction, conditional marginal bidding, and neighbor-based conflict resolution under limited communication. We prove that DAGBA guarantees per-epoch feasibility, finite-round convergence, and residual-energy safety. Theoretically, we identify a sequential-greedy regime where DAGBA recovers the classical $1/2$-approximation guarantee. For general executions with partial information, we derive a local-information-factor approximation bound and conservative bounds computable from the execution trace that quantify the degradation caused by local estimates and parallel fixing. Simulations on cooperative observation missions demonstrate that DAGBA achieves task-completion progress and utility close to centralized and complete-communication references, while improving communication efficiency and maintaining strict energy feasibility.
  </details>

- **[Strategic and Robust Task Allocation for Combat Objectives in Adversarial Multi-Agent Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34158)**  `arXiv:2611.34158`  
  _Jonas Peché, Dmitry Matveev, Vladimir Ciric, Lizaveta Sakalova, Günter Wallner_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Task allocation in contested-objective team games requires coordinated decisions under uncertainty, spatial constraints, and changing tactical conditions. In such settings, multiple agents must anticipate both teammate behavior and opponent actions. We study a hybrid predict-then-optimize approach for assigning controllable agents to objectives in real time. A masked multi-head model predicts tactical signals for each agent, including survival chance, local superiority, combat interaction, travel time, and objective contribution. These signals are combined with rule-based terms in a score matrix, and a minimum-cost flow solver computes coordinated global assignments constrained by capacity, occupancy, stability, and defensive strategies. Learning is limited to tactical scoring, while explicit rules and solver structure preserve controllability and interpretability. We evaluate the system using predictive metrics, offline assignment diagnostics, online A/B evaluation, and latency measurements. The system is an R\&D research prototype built on a commercial game and is not deployed in the shipped game. The results indicate that learned tactical estimates can support stable, feasible, and inspectable objective allocation under strict real-time constraints.
  </details>

- **[Post-Training Policy Replication for Strategy-Following Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning across Team Sizes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34035)**  `arXiv:2611.34035`

To reduce this computational cost, we introduce a team-size-independent observation architecture and reconstruct collective behavior by replicating a single trained policy across agents in teams of different sizes, thereby eliminating the need to train from scratch. Additionally, we evaluate warm-start retraining by initializing policy networks with a pre-trained policy to significantly lower computational overhead. In an object collection game, a policy trained in a four-agent team is deployed to teams of three to eight agents. Experiments demonstrate that training with the proposed aggregated observation matrix achieves performance comparable to that of the baseline method, sfDA7-X. Furthermore, policy replication preserves performance without substantial degradation in three- and five-agent teams, and warm-start retraining outperforms training from scratch while reducing required training episodes by up to 90%. Deployments to six- and eight-agent teams further confirm effective spatial region allocation following given instructions. These results demonstrate that the proposed method enables zero-shot collective behavior reconstruction via policy replication.
  </details>

- **[When Are Parallel Subagents Effective for Coding? An Empirical Study on Repository Construction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33893)**  `arXiv:2611.33893`  
  _Zhiheng Lyu, Chengyu Yin, Lingming Zhang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  LLM-based coding agents are increasingly used for long-horizon tasks such as building an entire program from a specification. Products like Codex and Claude Code let an agent delegate work to parallel subagents, multiplying run cost, yet it remains unclear whether and when delegation produces a better program. We compare a single agent with a main agent delegating to subagents on repository-construction tasks from NL2Repo and ProgramBench (which also provides an executable reference program). We compare scores at equal time and equal cost, run intervention experiments, and analyze fine-grained behavior. On randomly drawn tasks, parallel subagents raise hidden-test pass rates by only about 1 to 5 percentage points at up to 3.8x the cost of a single agent. Their gain is larger on hard tasks, where we find evidence of three mechanisms. Self-checking: with GPT-5.6 Sol, one sentence telling a single agent to probe the reference program first recovers most of this gain at a fraction of the cost; from GPT-5.6 Sol to GPT-6.1 Sol, the gain shrinks as single agents check their own work more. Fresh context: in extended runs, a single agent that periodically starts a new session with an empty conversation makes faster early progress in every comparison than one that resumes its conversation. Modularity: multi-agent runs produce more modular code (more files and shorter functions), closer to the upstream source. We observe similar patterns in a smaller replication with Opus 5.5 on Claude Code. Overall, subagents help when (i) a single agent stops checking too early, (ii) a long session keeps editing with little improvement, or (iii) modular code helps on the task; otherwise, they mainly add cost.
  </details>

- **[CypherMAS: Benchmarking Routing Reliability in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33242)**  `arXiv:2611.33242`  
  _Danil Kostromin, Andrey Sakhovskiy, Semen Budennyy_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs) distribute reasoning across specialized agents that must exchange messages and invoke tools reliably. Existing evaluations typically couple communication with open domain tasks, making it difficult to determine whether a failure arises from reasoning, malformed tool use, lost messages, or forgotten requests. Prior benchmarks do not isolate communication execution or measure routing redundancy against a known optimal path. We introduce CypherMAS, a synthetic benchmark that isolates communication and routing in fixed multi-agent graphs. Agents in chain, star, bipartite, or ring graphs route cyphered messages to remote peers holding the matching decoders; since the optimal route is known, redundant LLM calls can be measured and routing failures may be easily tracked. Across eleven open-weight models from 4B to 753B, small models fail at routing and tool use, dense models above 27B degrade with diameter, and successful runs exceed minimum LLM calls. These findings identify communication reliability as a distinct scaling bottleneck for multi-agent systems and provide a controlled diagnostic for complex multi-agent systems. The source code is freely available:this https URL.
  </details>

- **[Soft Decentralized Expected SARSA: Equilibrium Selection via Gradual Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33228)**  `arXiv:2611.33228`  
  _Giuseppe Martucci, Janusz M. Meylahn, Gurdal Arslan, Serdar Yuksel_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We introduce Soft Decentralized Expected SARSA (SDES), a modification of Decentralized Q-learning in which agents maintain persistent exploration and update their acting Q-values gradually rather than switching directly to newly learned best responses when updating. We prove convergence to $\epsilon$-greedy Nash equilibria in weakly acyclic stochastic games for sufficiently large batch sizes. We then show, in the repeated Prisoner's Dilemma with memory, that soft updating can reshape basins of attraction without changing the equilibrium set. In the deterministic limit, we derive analytical basin bounds governed by the Q-value differences between actions in the target policies and show that reducing the policy learning rate can favor either cooperative or competitive equilibria. These results suggest that soft updating is not merely a stabilization device but also a mechanism of equilibrium selection in decentralized learning.
  </details>

- **[GRASP: Graph Agentic Search over Propositions for Multi-hop Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16598)**  `arXiv:2605.16598`  
  _Stockton Jenkins, Ramya Korlakai Vinayak, Junjie Hu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Agentic retrieval improves multi-hop question answering by giving language models autonomy to iteratively gather evidence. Recent work augments these systems with knowledge graphs for structured traversal, but this combination introduces significant cost: expensive graph construction at index time and compounding token usage at inference time. We introduce Graph Agentic Search over Propositions (GRASP), an agentic system that simultaneously optimizes for high accuracy and minimal token usage in multi-hop question answering. Rather than executing a rigid, singular query, GRASP actively coordinates its retrieval strategy by decomposing multi-hop queries into dependency-aware plans. This enables GRASP to dynamically scale the number of sub-agents according to the complexity of the problem. Each sub-agent resolves its single-hop query by exploring a novel three-layer hierarchical graph of entities, propositions, and passages, using the entity layer for targeted traversal and the proposition layer for high-recall passage retrieval via reciprocal-rank voting. We evaluate GRASP on MuSiQue, 2WikiMultihopQA, and HotpotQA under two settings: open-corpus retrieval and extended context reasoning (LongBench). GRASP achieves the highest QA accuracy in the open retrieval setting on MuSiQue and 2Wiki while using 40-50 percent fewer tokens than IRCoT+HippoRAG2. Furthermore, GRASP leads on EM and F1 across all three datasets in the LongBench setting while using 30 percent fewer tokens than the next most accurate method. Finally, we introduce success economy - the amortized token cost per correct answer, weighted by difficulty - and advocate for efficiency-aware evaluation as a standard practice for agentic QA.
  </details>
